title: Zechariah - Introduction
content:
Introduction to Zechariah

Part 1: General Introduction

Outline of the Book of Zechariah

  1. Zechariah calls the returning nation of Israel to repent and return to Yahweh (1:1–6)
  2. The eight night visions (1:7–6:8)
    1. Yahweh sends his messengers throughout the whole earth (1:7–17)
    2. Four horns and four craftsmen (1:18–21)
    3. The measuring line (2:1–13)
    4. The priest in filthy clothes (3:1–10)
    5. The golden lampstand olive trees (4:1–14)
    6. The flying scroll (5:1–4)
    7. The woman in a basket (5:5–11)
    8. Four chariots (6:1–8)
  3. A crown for the high priest (6:9–15)
  4. Questions about fasting (7:1–8:23)
  5. Yahweh judge the nations and saves his people (9:1–11:17)
  6. Final message (12:1–14:21)
    1. Yahweh will finally defeat Israel’s enemies (12:1–9)
    2. Israel mourns for the one they pierced (12:10–14)
    3. Yahweh purifies Israel and removes false prophets (13:1–6)
    4. Yahweh comes as king (14:1–21)

Literary Structure

Many interpreters see Zechariah organized using chiasms—mirrored patterns where the beginning and end match, then the second and second-to-last parts match, and so on. Three larger sections show this design: the eight night visions (1:7–6:15), the two fasting messages (7:1–8:23), and the closing oracles (chapters 9–14). Smaller chiasms also appear within individual passages, such as 1:14–17 and 8:9–13.

What is the Book of Zechariah about?

Zechariah wrote to the people of Judah who returned from being exiled in Babylon. The people of Judah continued to sin, as their ancestors did before they went into exile. Zechariah called the people to repent and to obey Yahweh. And he called them to renew the covenant with Yahweh. Zechariah also prophesied about the Messiah and about Israel finally being victorious over her enemies.

How should the title of this book be translated?

This book traditionally has been titled “Zechariah” or “The Book of Zechariah.” Translators may decide to call it the “The Book About Zechariah” or “The Sayings of Zechariah.”

Who wrote the Book of Zechariah?

The prophet Zechariah wrote this book between 520 and 518 B.C.

Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

Did Zechariah prophesy before Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai?

Zechariah prophesied before the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He prophesied at the same time as Haggai and continued after Haggai.

Part 3: Important Translation Issues

What is the meaning of the term “Israel”?

The name “Israel” is used in many different ways in the Bible. Jacob was a son of Isaac. God changed Jacob’s name to Israel. The descendants of Jacob became a nation also called Israel. Eventually, the nation of Israel split into two kingdoms. The northern kingdom was named Israel. The southern kingdom was named Judah. Zechariah uses the term “Israel” to refer to both the nation of Israel and the northern kingdom of Israel.

What imagery does Zechariah use in reference to the Messiah?

Zechariah presented the Messiah as both a king and a shepherd. Zechariah said that the Messiah would come and deliver his people. However, the Messiah would also be pierced (12:10) and struck with the sword (13:7).

What does the phrase “that day” mean?

Zechariah often spoke of the last days by using the phrase “that day” or “in that day.” When referring to a future “day,” the translator should be aware that the author may be speaking about the last days. If your language wouldn’t use the repetition of “on that day” for stylistic emphasis, find a natural way to do it in your language.

title: Zechariah - Chapter 1 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 1 General Notes

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written in prose with imagery used throughout to portray Zechariah’s vision given by the Lord.

Some translations prefer to set apart quotations. The ULT and many other English translations set lines 1:3–6, 14–17, which are extended quotations, farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text.

The Eight Night-Visions as a Chiasm

Chapters 1:7–6:8 present eight visions arranged in a mirrored (chiastic) pattern: patrolling horses (1:7–17) match the closing chariot vision (6:1–8); the horns that scattered Judah (1:18–21) match the removal of wickedness in the basket vision (5:5–11); Jerusalem without walls (2:1–5) matches the scroll of judgment (5:1–4); and Joshua reclothed (3:1–10) matches the two anointed leaders, Joshua and Zerubbabel (4:1–14). This chapter contains the first two panels of that pattern.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Visions

This book contains a number of visions given to Zechariah. The images are not ones Zechariah actually saw; rather, they were given to him in a vision or dream. It is important for each of these visions to keep their given meanings and not be interpreted to mean any specific thing.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Date

Zechariah uses two separate dates in this first chapter. When compared to the book of Haggai, Zechariah’s prophecy was proclaimed just a few weeks after the prophecy of Haggai. However, the two men prophesied in two different places: Haggai was in Jerusalem, and Zechariah was somewhere outside of Jerusalem.

title: Zechariah 1:1 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ הַ⁠שְּׁמִינִ֔י בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֥ת שְׁתַּ֖יִם לְ⁠דָרְיָ֑וֶשׁ

"In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius"

If your language would not represent numbers in a form such as eighth and second, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In month eight in year two of Darius]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Zechariah 1:1 (#2)
content:
הָיָ֣ה דְבַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־זְכַרְיָה֙

"the word of Yahweh came to Zechariah"

Zechariah is using the word of Yahweh came to Zechariah as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh communicated a message to Zechariah.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh spoke his message to Zechariah] or [Yahweh gave his message to Zechariah]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 1:1 (#3)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ הַ⁠שְּׁמִינִ֔י בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֥ת שְׁתַּ֖יִם לְ⁠דָרְיָ֑וֶשׁ

"In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius"

Zechariah is using the phrase In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius to introduce a new event in the story (in this case, the very beginning). Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 1:2 (#1)
content:
קָצַ֧ף & קָֽצֶף

"was angry {with} anger"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [was extremely angry]

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 1:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֗ם כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"And you shall say to them, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall tell them that Yahweh of Armies says this]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Zechariah 1:3 (#2)
content:
שׁ֣וּבוּ אֵלַ֔⁠י

"Return to me"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s relationship with him were a place that they had physically left and could physically come back to. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be faithful to me again] or [Renew your commitment to me]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 1:3 (#3)
content:
נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

The term the declaration of Yahweh of Armies introduces a parenthetical affirmation of the source of this direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the authoritative source of direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 1:3 (#4)
content:
שׁ֣וּבוּ אֵלַ֔⁠י & וְ⁠אָשׁ֣וּב אֲלֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"Return to me & and I will return to you"

Here, Return to me introduces the first part of a possible condition. Yahweh will only do the thing in the second part, and I will return to you, if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If you return to me, then I will return to you]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Zechariah 1:3 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אָשׁ֣וּב אֲלֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"and I will return to you"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his renewed favor toward the people were a physical movement back to them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will be favorable to you again] or [and I will bless you again]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 1:4 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠דַּרְכֵי⁠כֶ֣ם הָ⁠רָעִ֔ים ו⁠מעלילי⁠כם הָֽ⁠רָעִ֑ים

"from your evil ways and your evil deeds"

The terms evil ways and evil deeds mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from all of your evil conduct]

See: Doublet

title: Zechariah 1:4 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠דַּרְכֵי⁠כֶ֣ם הָ⁠רָעִ֔ים

"from your evil ways"

Yahweh is speaking of how the ancestors lived as if that were a way or path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from your evil behavior]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 1:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א שָׁמְע֛וּ וְ⁠לֹֽא־הִקְשִׁ֥יבוּ

"But they did not hear, and they did not pay attention"

Yahweh uses the word But here to indicate a contrast between what the former prophets told the ancestors to do and what the ancestors actually did. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, they did not hear, and they did not pay attention]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 1:4 (#4)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and told them that Yahweh of Armies had said to]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Zechariah 1:4 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א שָׁמְע֛וּ וְ⁠לֹֽא־הִקְשִׁ֥יבוּ אֵלַ֖⁠י

"But they did not hear, and they did not pay attention to me"

The terms did not hear and did not pay attention mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [But they completely refused to obey me]

See: Doublet

title: Zechariah 1:5 (#1)
content:
אֲבֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶ֖ם אַיֵּה־הֵ֑ם

"Your fathers, where {are} they"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the ancestors are dead. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your fathers are no longer alive.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 1:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ֨⁠נְּבִאִ֔ים הַ⁠לְ⁠עוֹלָ֖ם יִֽחְיֽוּ

"And the prophets, do they live forever"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the prophets also died. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And the prophets did not live forever either.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 1:6 (#1)
content:
אַ֣ךְ ׀ דְּבָרַ֣⁠י וְ⁠חֻקַּ֗⁠י

"But my words and my statutes"

Yahweh uses the word But here to indicate a contrast between the mortality of the fathers and prophets and the enduring effect of God’s words and statutes. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, my words and my statutes]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 1:6 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֥וֹא הִשִּׂ֖יגוּ אֲבֹתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"did they not overtake your fathers"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that his words certainly did overtake the ancestors. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [they certainly overtook your fathers.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 1:6 (#3)
content:
דְּבָרַ֣⁠י וְ⁠חֻקַּ֗⁠י & הֲ⁠ל֥וֹא הִשִּׂ֖יגוּ אֲבֹתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"my words and my statutes & did they not overtake your fathers"

Yahweh is speaking of my words and my statutes as if they were living things that could pursue and catch people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my words and my statutes, … did they not come true for your fathers]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 1:6 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יָּשׁ֣וּבוּ וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֗וּ

"And they returned and said"

The pronoun they refers to the ancestors, not to the words and statutes mentioned earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And your ancestors repented and said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 1:6 (#5)
content:
כִּ⁠דְרָכֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ וּ⁠כְ⁠מַ֣עֲלָלֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"according to our ways and according to our deeds"

The ancestors are speaking of how they lived as if that were a way or path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to how we behaved and according to what we did]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 1:7 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠יוֹם֩ עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֜ה

"On the twenty-fourth day"

Zechariah is using the phrase On the twenty-fourth day to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 1:7 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠יוֹם֩ עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֜ה לְ⁠עַשְׁתֵּֽי־עָשָׂ֥ר חֹ֨דֶשׁ֙

"On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month"

Both twenty-fourth and eleventh are ordinal numbers. If your language would not represent a number in a ordinal form, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [On day twenty-four of month eleven]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Zechariah 1:7 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֥ת שְׁתַּ֖יִם לְ⁠דָרְיָ֑וֶשׁ

"in the second year of Darius"

The phrase in the second year uses an ordinal number. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as second, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year two of the reign of Darius]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Zechariah 1:7 (#4)
content:
הָיָ֣ה דְבַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־זְכַרְיָה֙

"the word of Yahweh came to Zechariah"

Zechariah is using the word of Yahweh came to Zechariah as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh communicated a message to Zechariah.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh spoke his message to Zechariah] or [Yahweh gave his message to Zechariah]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 1:7 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠נָּבִ֖יא לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"the prophet, saying"

The word saying normally introduces something Yahweh said. Here it introduces what Zechariah saw in a vision, which he describes in his own words starting in the next verse. If it would be unnatural in your language to use a speech word to introduce a vision, you could use a phrase that introduces a report or account instead, and you should not mark the vision as a quotation. Alternate translation: [the prophet. This is what Yahweh showed him:] or [the prophet, and this is what happened:]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 1:8 (#1)
content:
רָאִ֣יתִי ׀ הַ⁠לַּ֗יְלָה וְ⁠הִנֵּה

"I saw in the night, and behold"

Zechariah is using the phrase I saw in the night, and behold to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 1:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּה

"and behold"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and I saw]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 1:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֗עַן & וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"answered and said"

The terms answered and said together introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 1:10 (#2)
content:
אֵ֚לֶּה

"These"

The pronoun These refers to the horses and their riders that Yahweh sent to patrol the earth. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [These horses and riders]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 1:11 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעֲנ֞וּ

"And they answered"

The pronoun they refers to the horse riders who had been patrolling the earth, described in verse 8. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the riders answered]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 1:11 (#2)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעֲנ֞וּ & וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֖וּ

"And they answered & and they said"

The terms answered and said together introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 1:11 (#3)
content:
כָל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ יֹשֶׁ֥בֶת וְ⁠שֹׁקָֽטֶת

"all of the earth is sitting and is at rest"

The riders are speaking of all of the earth as if it were a living thing that could sit down and be quiet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the peoples of the earth are peaceful and calm]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 1:12 (#1)
content:
עַד־מָתַ֗י אַתָּה֙ לֹֽא־תְרַחֵ֣ם אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְ⁠אֵ֖ת עָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר זָעַ֔מְתָּה זֶ֖ה שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה

"until when & not have compassion on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah & these"

The angel of Yahweh is using the question form to urgently plead with God to show mercy. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please have compassion on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah with which you have been indignant these 70 years now!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 1:12 (#2)
content:
אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְ⁠אֵ֖ת עָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה

"on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah"

Here, Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah represents the people who live in those places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on the people of Jerusalem and the people of the cities of Judah]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 1:13 (#1)
content:
דְּבָרִ֖ים נִחֻמִֽים

"words of comfort"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of comfort, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [words that comforted him]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 1:14 (#1)
content:
קְרָ֣א לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת

"Call out, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Proclaim that Yahweh of Armies says this]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Zechariah 1:14 (#2)
content:
קִנֵּ֧אתִי לִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם וּ⁠לְ⁠צִיּ֖וֹן קִנְאָ֥ה גְדוֹלָֽה

"I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion {with} a great jealousy"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I have been very zealous for Jerusalem and for Zion]

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 1:14 (#3)
content:
קִנְאָ֥ה גְדוֹלָֽה

"with} a great jealousy"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of jealousy, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [indeed very jealous]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 1:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠קֶ֤צֶף גָּדוֹל֙ אֲנִ֣י קֹצֵ֔ף

"And {with} a great anger I, I am angry"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And I am very, very angry]

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 1:15 (#2)
content:
אֲנִ֣י קֹצֵ֔ף & אֲנִי֙ קָצַ֣פְתִּי

"I, I am angry & I, I was angry"

The pronoun I is repeated for emphasis in both clauses. You could translate Yahweh’s emphasis with a phrase that conveys strong personal involvement in your language. Alternate translation: [I myself am angry…I myself was angry]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 1:15 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֤ר אֲנִי֙ קָצַ֣פְתִּי מְּעָ֔ט וְ⁠הֵ֖מָּה עָזְר֥וּ לְ⁠רָעָֽה

"for I, I was angry {only} a little, but they helped toward the evil"

Yahweh uses the word but here to indicate a contrast between the limited extent of his anger and the excessive harm the nations inflicted. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for I was angry only a little, yet they made the harm far worse]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 1:15 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠רָעָֽה

"toward the evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to do what was harmful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 1:16 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵ֞ן

"Therefore"

The term translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because of this]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 1:16 (#2)
content:
שַׁ֤בְתִּי לִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ בְּֽ⁠רַחֲמִ֔ים

"I have returned to Jerusalem with compassions"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his renewed favor toward Jerusalem were a physical journey back to the city. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have again shown favor to Jerusalem with mercy] or [I have once again been gracious to Jerusalem]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 1:16 (#3)
content:
בְּֽ⁠רַחֲמִ֔ים

"with compassions"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of compassions, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while acting mercifully to her people]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 1:16 (#4)
content:
בֵּיתִ⁠י֙ יִבָּ֣נֶה בָּ֔⁠הּ

"My house will be built in her"

The expression My house will be built in her is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the people of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [the people will build my house in her]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 1:16 (#5)
content:
ו⁠קוה יִנָּטֶ֖ה עַל־יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

"and a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem"

The expression a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the builders. Alternate translation: [and the builders will stretch out a measuring line over Jerusalem]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 1:16 (#6)
content:
ו⁠קוה

"and a measuring line"

A measuring line is a kind of rope or cord that builders stretch out to measure distances when constructing or planning a building or city. If your readers would not be familiar with what a measuring line is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and a measuring rope]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 1:17 (#1)
content:
עָרַ֖⁠י

"My cities"

Here, My cities represents the people who live in those cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The people living in my cities]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 1:17 (#2)
content:
קְרָ֣א לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר

"call out, saying"

There are three levels of quotation here. The angel of Yahweh is speaking to Zechariah (level 1) and telling him to proclaim a message (level 2), which itself quotes what Yahweh of Armies says (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a third-level quotation.

See: Quote Markings

title: Zechariah 1:17 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠טּ֑וֹב

"from goodness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of goodness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from good things]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 1:18 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֥א אֶת־עֵינַ֖⁠י וָ⁠אֵ֑רֶא

"my eyes and I saw"

Zechariah is using the phrase And I lifted up my eyes and I saw to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 1:18 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֥א אֶת־עֵינַ֖⁠י

"my eyes"

Zechariah is using And I lifted up my eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “I looked” or “I directed my attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I looked up] or [And I directed my gaze upward]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 1:18 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֖ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הִנֵּ֖ה"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and there I saw]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 1:19 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠קְּרָנוֹת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר זֵר֣וּ אֶת־יְהוּדָ֔ה

"the horns that scattered Judah"

Here, the horns represents the military power of the nations that attacked God’s people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the powerful nations that scattered the people of Judah]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 1:19 (#2)
content:
אֶת־יְהוּדָ֔ה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִ⁠ירוּשָׁלָֽם

"Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem"

Here, Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem represents the people who lived in those nations and that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Judah, the people of Israel, and the people of Jerusalem]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#1)
content:
אֵ֥לֶּה & אֵ֣לֶּה הַ⁠קְּרָנ֞וֹת & וַ⁠יָּבֹ֤אוּ אֵ֨לֶּה֙

"are} these & These {are} the horns & And these have come"

The word These is used three times in this verse with two different referents. The first and third these refers to the craftsmen. The second these refers to the horns, that is, the powerful nations. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [are these craftsmen … These horns are the nations … And these craftsmen have come]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠פִי

"according to the mouth of"

The angel is using according to the mouth of as a common expression of the culture to mean “so that.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the extent that]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#3)
content:
אִישׁ֙ לֹא־נָשָׂ֣א רֹאשׁ֔⁠וֹ

"a man {who} has not lifted up his head"

The angel is using has not lifted up his head as a common expression of the culture to mean “no one was able to resist or act with confidence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [no one was able to resist them] or [no one dared to oppose them]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יָּבֹ֤אוּ אֵ֨לֶּה֙ לְ⁠הַחֲרִ֣יד אֹתָ֔⁠ם

"And these have come to terrify them"

The term translated as And here indicates that what follows is the result or purpose of what came before. The craftsmen have come in order to terrify the nations that scattered Judah. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [So these have come to terrify them]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#5)
content:
אֶת־קַרְנ֣וֹת הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֗ם

"the horns of the nations"

Here, the horns of the nations represents the military power of those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the armies of the nations]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#6)
content:
הַ⁠נֹּשְׂאִ֥ים קֶ֛רֶן אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ יְהוּדָ֖ה

"the ones lifting up a horn against the land of Judah"

Here, lifting up a horn represents exercising aggressive military power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones using their military power against the land of Judah]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 1:21 (#7)
content:
אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ יְהוּדָ֖ה

"against the land of Judah"

Here, the land of Judah represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against the people of Judah]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah - Chapter 2 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 2 General Notes

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is introduced in prose with imagery used in the rest of the chapter to portray Zechariah’s third vision about measuring lines given by the Lord.

Some translations prefer to set apart quotations. The ULT and many other English translations set the lines of 2:4–13, which are extended quotations, farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Visions

This book contains a number of visions given to Zechariah, so the images are not ones Zechariah actually saw, but were ones given to him in a vision or dream. It is important for each of these visions to keep their meanings and not be interpreted to mean any specific thing. Please be careful to translate each of the terms in your language.

title: Zechariah 2:1 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֥א עֵינַ֛⁠י וָ⁠אֵ֖רֶא וְ⁠הִנֵּה

"And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold"

The phrase And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold is a way that Zechariah introduces each new vision in his book. Your language may have its own way of introducing a new vision or important event in a narrative.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 2:1 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֥א עֵינַ֛⁠י

"And I lifted up my eyes"

The expression I lifted up my eyes was a common expression meaning “I looked up” or “I looked intently.” If this expression does not communicate well in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I looked up]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 2:1 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּה

"and behold"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and I was surprised to see]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 2:1 (#4)
content:
חֶ֥בֶל מִדָּֽה

"a rope of measuring"

Zechariah is using the possessive form to describe a rope that is used for measuring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the possessive form with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a string for measuring]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 2:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֗ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הִנֵּ֗ה"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 2:3 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠קְרָאתֽ⁠וֹ

"to meet him"

The pronoun him refers to the angel who had been speaking with Zechariah, not to the man with the measuring line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that more clearly. Alternate translation: [to meet the interpreting angel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔⁠ו

"And he said to him"

Here, he refers to the second angel, and him refers to the angel who had been speaking with Zechariah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that more clearly. Alternate translation: [And the second angel said to the first angel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#2)
content:
רֻ֗ץ דַּבֵּ֛ר אֶל־הַ⁠נַּ֥עַר הַלָּ֖ז לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"Run, speak to that young man, saying"

If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. For example, you could express the inner quotation as an indirect quotation.

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠נַּ֥עַר הַלָּ֖ז

"that young man"

The phrase that young man likely refers to the man with the measuring line from verse 1. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that more clearly. Alternate translation: [the young man who was going to measure Jerusalem]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#4)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"saying"

The word saying introduces a quotation. Use a natural form for introducing a quotation in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#5)
content:
פְּרָזוֹת֙ תֵּשֵׁ֣ב יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם

"Jerusalem will be inhabited {as} open areas"

The second angel is speaking of Jerusalem as if it would be like open areas without walls, meaning the city will have so many inhabitants that people will overflow beyond its walls. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Jerusalem will be like an unwalled city]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#6)
content:
מֵ⁠רֹ֥ב אָדָ֛ם וּ⁠בְהֵמָ֖ה

"because of the multitude of man and beast"

If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the abstract noun multitude in another way. Alternate translation: [the many people and animals]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 2:4 (#7)
content:
אָדָ֛ם וּ⁠בְהֵמָ֖ה

"man and beast"

The second angel is referring to all living creatures by naming two broad categories, man and beast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people and animals of every kind]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 2:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֤י אֶֽהְיֶה־לָּ⁠הּ֙

"And I, I will be for her"

Here, the pronoun I is repeated for emphasis. Yahweh is emphasizing his personal commitment to protect Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And I, even I, will be for her]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:5 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the abstract noun declaration in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh declares]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 2:5 (#3)
content:
ח֥וֹמַת אֵ֖שׁ סָבִ֑יב

"a wall of fire all around"

Yahweh is speaking of his protection of Jerusalem as if he were a wall of fire all around it, meaning he will powerfully protect the city on every side. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a powerful defense all around]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 2:5 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠כָב֖וֹד אֶֽהְיֶ֥ה בְ⁠תוֹכָֽ⁠הּ

"and for glory I will be in her midst"

If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the abstract noun glory in another way. Alternate translation: [to show how glorious I am, I will be in her midst]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 2:5 (#5)
content:
בְ⁠תוֹכָֽ⁠הּ

"in her midst"

Here, her refers to Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that more clearly. Alternate translation: [in the midst of Jerusalem]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:6 (#1)
content:
ה֣וֹי ה֗וֹי

"Woe! Woe"

The exclamation Woe! is repeated for emphasis to express urgency and warning. If your language has its own way of expressing an urgent warning, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [Listen! Listen!]

See: Exclamations

title: Zechariah 2:6 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צָפ֖וֹן

"from the land of the north"

Yahweh is using the land of the north to refer to Babylon, since the Babylonians came from the north to invade Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the land of Babylon, in the north]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 2:6 (#3)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea behind the abstract noun declaration in another way. Alternate translation: [this is what Yahweh says]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 2:6 (#4)
content:
כְּ⁠אַרְבַּ֞ע רוּח֧וֹת הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֛יִם פֵּרַ֥שְׂתִּי אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם

"as the four winds of the heavens, I have spread you out"

Yahweh compares the way he scattered his people to the way the four winds of the heavens blow in every direction. If this comparison does not communicate well in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have scattered you to every part of the earth]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 2:7 (#1)
content:
ה֥וֹי צִיּ֖וֹן

"Woe, Zion"

The exclamation Woe expresses an urgent call. If your language has its own way of expressing an urgent call, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [Listen, Zion!]

See: Exclamations

title: Zechariah 2:7 (#2)
content:
צִיּ֖וֹן

"Zion"

Here, Zion represents the people who live in Jerusalem. Yahweh is calling the exiled people of Jerusalem to escape from Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state that plainly. Alternate translation: [you people of Zion]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 2:7 (#3)
content:
בַּת־בָּבֶֽל

"the daughter of Babylon"

Yahweh is using the daughter of Babylon as a common expression to refer to the people of Babylon. If this expression does not communicate well in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Babylon]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 2:8 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י כֹ֣ה אָמַר֮ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָאוֹת֒

"For thus says Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase For thus says Yahweh of Armies introduces an indirect quotation of what Yahweh says. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing indirect quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 2:8 (#2)
content:
אַחַ֣ר כָּב֔וֹד שְׁלָחַ֕⁠נִי

"after glory he has sent me"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in order to glorify himself, he has sent me]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 2:8 (#3)
content:
שְׁלָחַ֕⁠נִי

"he has sent me"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun me refers to the prophetic speaker. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has sent me, his prophet]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:8 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠נֹּגֵ֣עַ בָּ⁠כֶ֔ם נֹגֵ֖עַ בְּ⁠בָבַ֥ת עֵינֽ⁠וֹ

"the one touching you is touching the apple of his eye"

Yahweh is using the one touching you is touching the apple of his eye as a common expression of the culture to mean “harming you is harming what is most precious to him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who harms you harms what Yahweh treasures most]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 2:9 (#1)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֨י

"behold"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look, I am waving my hand over them]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 2:9 (#2)
content:
מֵנִ֤יף אֶת־יָדִ⁠י֙ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"I am waving my hand over them"

Here, my hand represents Yahweh’s power to punish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to strike them with my power]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 2:9 (#3)
content:
יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁלָחָֽ⁠נִי

"Yahweh of Armies has sent me"

The pronoun me refers to the prophetic speaker. This statement is outside Yahweh’s direct speech. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies has sent me, his prophet]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:10 (#1)
content:
רָנִּ֥י וְ⁠שִׂמְחִ֖י

"Sing and rejoice"

The terms Sing and rejoice mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Celebrate with great joy]

See: Doublet

title: Zechariah 2:10 (#2)
content:
בַּת־צִיּ֑וֹן

"daughter of Zion"

Yahweh is using daughter of Zion as a common expression of the culture to refer to the people of Jerusalem. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of Zion]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 2:10 (#3)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִי

"behold, I am"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [watch]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 2:10 (#4)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of declaration, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this is what Yahweh has declared]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 2:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נִלְווּ֩ גוֹיִ֨ם רַבִּ֤ים אֶל־יְהוָה֙

"And many nations will join themselves to Yahweh"

By join themselves to Yahweh, Zechariah means become worshipers of Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And people from many nations will worship Yahweh like the Israelites]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 2:11 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֔וּא

"in that day"

Yahweh is using the term day to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See the Introduction to Zechariah for a discussion of the phrase “in that day.”

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 2:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יָדַ֕עַתְּ כִּי־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁלָחַ֥⁠נִי אֵלָֽיִ⁠ךְ

"And you will know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you"

Here the pronoun you is singular and refers to the people of Zion, and the pronoun me refers to the prophetic speaker. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And you, people of Zion, will know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me, his prophet, to you]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 2:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָחַ֨ל & אֶת־יְהוּדָה֙ חֶלְק֔⁠וֹ

"will inherit Judah {as} his portion"

The word translated as will inherit means to take formal, permanent possession of something as one’s rightful property. It does not imply that a previous owner has died. If the word you use for will inherit would give your readers that wrong impression, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [will claim Judah as his possession]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 2:12 (#2)
content:
אַדְמַ֣ת הַ⁠קֹּ֑דֶשׁ

"the land of holiness"

title: Zechariah - Chapter 3 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 3 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents Zechariah’s fourth night vision: a heavenly courtroom scene in which Joshua the priest stands before the angel of Yahweh while the adversary accuses him (vv.1–5), followed by a prophetic oracle about “the Branch” and the removal of iniquity (vv.6–10).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Clothing as a Symbol of Moral State

Filthy garments represent sin and defilement, while clean garments and a clean turban represent purification and restored priestly authority.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Nested Quotation Structure

Verses 7–10 contain three levels of quotation: the angel of Yahweh quotes Yahweh of Armies, whose speech includes both a conditional promise and a messianic oracle.

title: Zechariah 3:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּרְאֵ֗⁠נִי

Zechariah is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

אֶת־יְהוֹשֻׁ֨עַ֙ הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֣ן הַ⁠גָּד֔וֹל

"Joshua the high priest"

Zechariah is introducing Joshua the high priest as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a man named Joshua who served as the high priest]

content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠שָּׂטָ֛ן

"and the adversary"

title: Zechariah 3:1 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יַּרְאֵ֗⁠נִי

"And he made me see"

The pronoun he could refer to (1) Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh made me see], or (2) the angel that was speaking to Zechariah. Alternate translation: [The angel made me see]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 3:1 (#5)
content:
עֹמֵ֕ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֑ה

"standing to the face of the angel of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents “in the presence of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [standing in the presence of the angel of Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 3:2 (#1)
content:
יִגְעַ֨ר יְהוָ֤ה בְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠שָּׂטָ֔ן וְ⁠יִגְעַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠ךָ֔ הַ⁠בֹּחֵ֖ר בִּ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם

"May Yahweh rebuke you, the adversary, and may Yahweh who is choosing Jerusalem rebuke you"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [May I, Yahweh, rebuke you, the adversary, and may I, Yahweh who is choosing Jerusalem, rebuke you]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 3:2 (#2)
content:
יִגְעַ֨ר יְהוָ֤ה בְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠שָּׂטָ֔ן וְ⁠יִגְעַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠ךָ֔ הַ⁠בֹּחֵ֖ר בִּ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם

"May Yahweh rebuke you, the adversary, and may Yahweh who is choosing Jerusalem rebuke you"

Yahweh is expressing what he desires to happen to the adversary. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I rebuke you, the adversary, and I, Yahweh who is choosing Jerusalem, rebuke you]

See: Third-Person Imperatives

title: Zechariah 3:2 (#3)
content:
יִגְעַ֨ר יְהוָ֤ה בְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠שָּׂטָ֔ן וְ⁠יִגְעַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠ךָ֔ הַ⁠בֹּחֵ֖ר בִּ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם

"May Yahweh rebuke you, the adversary, and may Yahweh who is choosing Jerusalem rebuke you"

These two phrases May Yahweh rebuke you, the adversary and may Yahweh who is choosing Jerusalem rebuke you mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Certainly, may Yahweh rebuke you, the adversary]

See: Parallelism

title: Zechariah 3:2 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֧וֹא זֶ֦ה א֖וּד מֻצָּ֥ל מֵ⁠אֵֽשׁ

"Is} this not a firebrand rescued from the fire"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that Joshua has indeed been rescued from destruction. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely this is a firebrand rescued from the fire!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 3:2 (#5)
content:
א֖וּד מֻצָּ֥ל מֵ⁠אֵֽשׁ

"a firebrand rescued from the fire"

Yahweh is speaking as if Joshua were a firebrand rescued from the fire. He means that Joshua has been barely saved from destruction. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one who has been barely saved from destruction]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:2 (#6)
content:
א֖וּד מֻצָּ֥ל מֵ⁠אֵֽשׁ

"a firebrand rescued from the fire"

The expression rescued is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a firebrand that God rescued from the fire]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 3:3 (#1)
content:
וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֕עַ הָיָ֥ה לָבֻ֖שׁ בְּגָדִ֣ים צוֹאִ֑ים וְ⁠עֹמֵ֖ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠מַּלְאָֽךְ

"was clothed {in} filthy & and standing to the face of"

Zechariah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

title: Zechariah 3:3 (#2)
content:
הָיָ֥ה לָבֻ֖שׁ בְּגָדִ֣ים צוֹאִ֑ים

"was clothed {in} filthy"

Zechariah is speaking as if Joshua’s sinfulness were filthy garments that he was wearing. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was wearing filthy clothes signifying sin and guilt] or [was deeply sinful]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:3 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עֹמֵ֖ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠מַּלְאָֽךְ

"and standing to the face of"

Here, to the face of represents “in the presence of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [standing in the presence of the angel]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֣עַן וַ⁠יֹּ֗אמֶר

"And he answered and said"

The pronoun he refers to the angel of Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the angel of Yahweh answered and said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠עֹמְדִ֤ים לְ⁠פָנָי⁠ו֙

"the ones standing to the face of him"

Here, to the face of represents “in the presence of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [those who stood before him]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#3)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר

"saying"

The term saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#4)
content:
הָסִ֛ירוּ הַ⁠בְּגָדִ֥ים הַ⁠צֹּאִ֖ים מֵ⁠עָלָ֑י⁠ו

"Remove the filthy garments from upon him"

The angel of Yahweh is speaking as if Joshua’s sin were filthy garments that could be removed. He means that God is taking away Joshua’s sin. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take away Joshua’s sin from him]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֗י⁠ו

"And he said to him"

The pronoun he refers to the angel of Yahweh, and him refers to Joshua. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the angel of Yahweh said to Joshua]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#6)
content:
רְאֵ֨ה

"See"

The angel of Yahweh is using the term See as an expression to focus Joshua’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention!]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#7)
content:
עֲוֺנֶ֔⁠ךָ

"your iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wrong things you have done]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#8)
content:
הֶעֱבַ֤רְתִּי מֵ⁠עָלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ עֲוֺנֶ֔⁠ךָ

"I have caused your iniquity to pass away from you"

The angel of Yahweh is speaking as if Joshua’s iniquity were a physical object that could be caused to pass away from him. He means that God has forgiven Joshua’s sin. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have forgiven your sin] Alternate translation: [I have forgiven your sin]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:4 (#9)
content:
וְ⁠הַלְבֵּ֥שׁ אֹתְ⁠ךָ֖ מַחֲלָצֽוֹת

"and I will clothe you {with} fine clothing"

The angel of Yahweh is speaking as if Joshua’s restored condition were fine clothing that he could put on. He means that God is restoring Joshua to a state of purity and honor. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will restore you to a state of purity and honor]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּשִׂימוּ֩ הַ⁠צָּנִ֨יף הַ⁠טָּה֜וֹר עַל־רֹאשׁ֗⁠וֹ וַ⁠יַּלְבִּשֻׁ֨⁠הוּ֙ בְּגָדִ֔ים

"And they set the clean turban on his head and clothed him {with} garments"

Setting a clean turban on Joshua’s head and clothing him with garments was a symbolic action by which the angels showed that Joshua was being restored to his priestly office. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [they set the clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments, showing that Joshua was being restored to his priestly office]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Zechariah 3:5 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֹמַ֕ר

"And I said"

The pronoun I refers to Zechariah, who is interjecting into the vision. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then I, Zechariah, said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 3:5 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה עֹמֵֽד

"and the angel of Yahweh was standing {by"

Zechariah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Zechariah 3:6 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

The term saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#1)
content:
כֹּה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת אִם־בִּ⁠דְרָכַ֤⁠י תֵּלֵךְ֙

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies, ‘If you will walk in my ways"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Here the angel is quoting Yahweh of Armies, whose words form a second level of quotation within the angel’s speech. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies has said: “If you will walk in my ways] or [Yahweh of Armies says that if you will walk in his ways]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#2)
content:
כֹּה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase Thus says Yahweh of Armies introduces a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase in exactly this way.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠דְרָכַ֤⁠י תֵּלֵךְ֙

"you will walk in my ways"

Yahweh is speaking as if obeying him were walking along a path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you obey my commands]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#4)
content:
אֶת־מִשְׁמַרְתִּ֣⁠י תִשְׁמֹ֔ר

"you will keep my charge"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#5)
content:
תָּדִ֣ין אֶת־בֵּיתִ֔⁠י

"will judge my house"

Yahweh is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a house in which he lived. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will oversee my temple]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֤י לְ⁠ךָ֙ מַהְלְכִ֔ים בֵּ֥ין הָ⁠עֹמְדִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה

"and I will give to you access among these who are standing {here"

Yahweh is speaking as if the privilege of coming into his presence were physical access to walk among the angels. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will allow you to be near me like these angels who are standing here]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:7 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֤י לְ⁠ךָ֙ מַהְלְכִ֔ים

"and I will give to you access"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of access, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will allow you to be]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 3:8 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠יֹּשְׁבִ֣ים לְ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"to the face of you"

Here, to the face of represents “in the presence of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who are sitting in the presence of you]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 3:8 (#2)
content:
אַנְשֵׁ֥י מוֹפֵ֖ת

"a sign"

Yahweh is using men of a sign as a common expression of the culture to mean “men whose lives serve as signs pointing to future events.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [men who are living signs pointing to what is to come]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 3:8 (#3)
content:
כִּֽי־אַנְשֵׁ֥י מוֹפֵ֖ת הֵ֑מָּה כִּֽי־הִנְ⁠נִ֥י

"a sign & behold"

Here, for marks Yahweh’s bringing of his servant the Branch as the goal or purpose of Joshua and his companions being men of a sign. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Zechariah 3:8 (#4)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֥י

"behold"

Yahweh is using the term behold to focus Joshua’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 3:8 (#5)
content:
צֶֽמַח

"the Branch"

Yahweh is speaking as if the future messianic king were a Branch growing from a family line. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the king who will come from the family line of David]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֣ה

"behold"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [notice]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוֹשֻׁ֔עַ

"to the face of Joshua"

Here, to the face of represents “in front of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Joshua]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#3)
content:
שִׁבְעָ֣ה עֵינָ֑יִם

"are} seven eyes"

Here, seven eyes represents God’s complete and watchful awareness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are seven facets that represent God’s complete awareness of everything]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#4)
content:
מְפַתֵּ֣חַ פִּתֻּחָ֗⁠הּ

"I am engraving its engraving"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#5)
content:
נְאֻם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

The expression the declaration of Yahweh of Armies is a prophetic attestation formula that affirms the authority of what is being said. In your translation, use a natural way of representing this kind of affirmation in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this expression in exactly this way.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠מַשְׁתִּ֛י אֶת־עֲוֺ֥ן הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ־הַ⁠הִ֖יא בְּ⁠י֥וֹם אֶחָֽד

"and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day"

Yahweh is speaking as if the iniquity of the land were a physical object that he could remove. He means that he will forgive the sin of the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will forgive the sin of that land]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:9 (#7)
content:
אֶת־עֲוֺ֥ן

"the iniquity of"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in 3:4. Alternate translation: [the wrong things that the people have done in]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 3:10 (#1)
content:
אֶל־תַּ֥חַת גֶּ֖פֶן וְ⁠אֶל־תַּ֥חַת תְּאֵנָֽה

"to under {his} vine and to under {his} fig tree"

Yahweh is speaking as if the peace and prosperity of the future age were sitting under a vine and fig tree. This was a common image representing security and contentment. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to enjoy calm prosperity together]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 3:10 (#2)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ לְ⁠רֵעֵ֑⁠הוּ

"each man to his neighbor"

The masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person to their neighbor]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah - Chapter 4 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 4 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Zechariah 4 is the fifth of eight night visions. The chapter moves from a prophetic vision (a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees) to an explanation, then to an oracle declaring that Zerubbabel will complete the temple “not by might and not by power, but by my Spirit,” and concludes with the identification of the two olive trees as those set apart to serve the Lord of all the earth.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Temple Furniture as Symbol

The lampstand echoes the tabernacle menorah (Exodus 25:31–40). Seven lamps and continuous olive oil flowing through golden pipes symbolized God’s provision for continuous worship and the Spirit’s empowering presence.

Anointing and Divine Empowering

“Sons of the fresh oil” is an idiom for those set apart for special service. Olive oil consecrated kings and priests; here it represents the Spirit enabling Zerubbabel and his community to complete the rebuilding work.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Quotations

Verses 6–10 contain a series of quotes in which it is difficult to discern who is speaking. The ULT suggests:

  • the angel speaks from 6–10
  • the angel quotes Yahweh in the middle of verse 6 and beginning of verse 9
  • the angel prophetically quotes the people’s reaction at the end of verse 7
  • the angel, not Zechariah, is the speaker who received the word of Yahweh in verse 8
  • the “me” at the end of verse 9 refers to the angel, this is probably the most contested point, scholars are divided as to if this is Zechariah, the angel speaking to him, or the Angel of Yahweh (read as Jesus)

If there is a translation in your area, you may wish to follow its decisions regarding speakers in this section. If not, you may wish to follow the ULT.

Mountains as Obstacles

Verse 7 calls a great mountain to become a plain, representing political and practical obstacles dissolving so that Zerubbabel can set the capstone in place.

title: Zechariah - Chapter 5 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 5 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents two visions in which an angel interprets what Zechariah sees. The first vision (verses 1–4) shows a flying scroll carrying a divine curse against thieves and false swearers. The second vision (verses 5–11) shows evil personified as a woman sealed inside an ephah and carried away to Shinar.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Personification of Wickedness

The angel identifies the woman inside the ephah as “the wickedness,” using a human figure to represent the community’s sin. Translators should preserve this identification without reducing it to a mere symbol.

Ancient Measurements

The chapter refers to cubits (verse 2) and the ephah (verses 6–10). These measurement units may need explanatory notes for readers unfamiliar with ancient systems.

title: Zechariah 5:1 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֖ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הִנֵּ֖ה"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and I saw]

title: Zechariah 5:2 (#1)
content:
עֶשְׂרִ֣ים בָּֽ⁠אַמָּ֔ה & עֶ֥שֶׂר בָּ⁠אַמָּֽה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: עֶשְׂרִ֣ים בָּֽ⁠אַמָּ֔ה & עֶ֥שֶׂר בָּ⁠אַמָּֽה"

A cubit was a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 45 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the dimensions of the scroll in modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [10 meters … 5 meters]

See: Biblical Distance

title: Zechariah 5:3 (#4)
content:
כָל־הַ⁠גֹּנֵ֗ב

"everyone"

The angel is not referring to a specific person who is stealing. He means anyone who steals in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone who steals]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 5:3 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠זֶּה֙ & מִ⁠זֶּ֖ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: מִ⁠זֶּה֙ & מִ⁠זֶּ֖ה"

The implication is that from this and from this refer to the two sides of the scroll, one side addressing those who steal and the other side addressing those who swear falsely. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on this side of the scroll … on the other side of the scroll]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 5:3 (#6)
content:
נִקָּ֔ה וְ⁠כָל־הַ⁠נִּ֨שְׁבָּ֔ע מִ⁠זֶּ֖ה כָּמ֥וֹ⁠הָ נִקָּֽה

"and everyone"

The expression has been cleared is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has cleared him, and everyone who is swearing from this side, according to it, Yahweh has also cleared]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#1)
content:
נְאֻם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase declaration of Yahweh of Armies identifies the speaker of the direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the speaker of a direct quotation in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase as an interruption within the quotation.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בָ֨אָה֙ & וְ⁠לָ֨נֶה֙ & וְ⁠כִלַּ֖תּ⁠וּ

"and it will come & And it will spend the night & and will consume it"

The pronoun it refers to the curse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the curse will come … And the curse will spend the night … and the curse will consume the house]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁמִ֖⁠י

"by my name"

Here, my name represents Yahweh’s person and authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by my name and authority]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠גַּנָּ֔ב & הַ⁠נִּשְׁבָּ֥ע בִּ⁠שְׁמִ֖⁠י לַ⁠שָּׁ֑קֶר

"the thief & the one swearing by my name to falsehood"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific thief or a specific person swearing by his name to falsehood. He means any such person in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people who steal … people who swear falsely by my name]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠נִּשְׁבָּ֥ע בִּ⁠שְׁמִ֖⁠י

"the one swearing by my name"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of falsehood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one falsely swearing by my name]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠לָ֨נֶה֙ בְּ⁠ת֣וֹךְ בֵּית֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠כִלַּ֖תּ⁠וּ וְ⁠אֶת־עֵצָ֥י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־אֲבָנָֽי⁠ו

"And it will spend the night in the midst of his house and will consume it, and its timbers, and its stones"

Yahweh is speaking of the curse as if it were a living thing that could spend the night in the midst of someone’s house and consume a house and its timbers and its stones. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will remain in his house and will destroy it, and its timbers and its stones]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 5:4 (#7)
content:
בֵּית֔⁠וֹ

"his house"

The pronoun his refers to each person who steals or swears falsely, as mentioned earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the house of the one who sinned]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 5:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֕א הַ⁠מַּלְאָ֖ךְ הַ⁠דֹּבֵ֣ר בִּ֑⁠י

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֕א הַ⁠מַּלְאָ֖ךְ הַ⁠דֹּבֵ֣ר בִּ֑⁠י"

Zechariah is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 5:5 (#2)
content:
שָׂ֣א נָ֤א עֵינֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ וּ⁠רְאֵ֔ה

"now your eyes and see"

The angel is using Lift up now your eyes and see as a common expression of the culture to mean “look up and pay attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look up now and pay attention to]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 5:6 (#1)
content:
עֵינָ֖⁠ם

"their eye"

The pronoun their refers to the people of the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people’s eye]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 5:6 (#2)
content:
עֵינָ֖⁠ם

"their eye"

The phrase their eye is a translation of the written text in the original language. Some ancient translations, however, read “their iniquity” instead. You may want to follow this alternative reading in your translation. Alternate translation: [their iniquity]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Zechariah 5:6 (#3)
content:
הָֽ⁠אֵיפָה֙

"the ephah"

An ephah was a unit of dry volume equivalent to about 22 liters or nearly two thirds of a bushel. Here it refers to a large measuring container. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Volume

title: Zechariah 5:6 (#4)
content:
עֵינָ֖⁠ם בְּ⁠כָל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"their eye & the earth"

Here, their eye could mean: (1) their appearance, meaning the ephah represents what the people are doing throughout the land. Alternate translation: [what they are doing throughout all the earth] (2) their iniquity, since the words for “eye” and “iniquity” are similar in the original language. Alternate translation: [how they are sinning throughout all the earth]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 5:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Then, look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 5:7 (#2)
content:
כִּכַּ֥ר עֹפֶ֖רֶת

"lead"

Zechariah is using the possessive form to describe a disk that is made of lead. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a lead disk]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 5:7 (#3)
content:
כִּכַּ֥ר עֹפֶ֖רֶת נִשֵּׂ֑את

"lead"

The expression was being lifted up is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone lifted up a disk of lead]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 5:8 (#1)
content:
זֹ֣את הָ⁠רִשְׁעָ֔ה

"This {is"

The angel is referring to the woman in the previous verse as wickedness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This woman embodies wickedness]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 5:8 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠רִשְׁעָ֔ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: הָ⁠רִשְׁעָ֔ה"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wickedness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how wicked they are]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 5:8 (#3)
content:
פִּֽי⁠הָ

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: פִּֽי⁠הָ"

Zechariah is using its mouth as a common expression of the culture to mean “its opening.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [its opening]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 5:9 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֨א עֵינַ֜⁠י וָ⁠אֵ֗רֶא

"my eyes and I saw"

Zechariah is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 5:9 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֨א עֵינַ֜⁠י

"my eyes"

See how you translated the similar expression in 5:1.

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 5:9 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּה֩

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הִנֵּה֩"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 5:9 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠חֲסִידָ֑ה

"the stork"

A stork is a kind of large water bird with long legs, a long beak, and large, powerful wings. If your readers would not be familiar with what a stork is, you could use the name of a similar large bird that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a large water bird]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 5:9 (#5)
content:
כְנָפַ֖יִם כְּ⁠כַנְפֵ֣י הַ⁠חֲסִידָ֑ה

"wings & the stork"

The point of this comparison is that just as the wings of the stork are large and powerful, so the wings of these two women were large and powerful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [wings as large and powerful as those of a stork]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 5:11 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֽוֹת

"To build"

Here, To build marks building a house for the woman in the land of Shinar as the goal or purpose of taking the ephah there. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Zechariah 5:11 (#2)
content:
לָ֥⁠הֿ

"for her"
