The pronoun her refers to the woman who represents wickedness. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for the woman who represents wickedness]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 5:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הוּכַ֛ן

"And it will be established"

The expression it will be established is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And they will establish it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 5:11 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הֻנִּ֥יחָה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הֻנִּ֥יחָה"

The expression she will be set down is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the two women. Alternate translation: [and they will set her down]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 5:11 (#5)
content:
עַל־מְכֻנָתָֽ⁠הּ

"on her base"

A base is a kind of platform or pedestal on which something is placed for support or display. If your readers would not be familiar with what a base is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [on her stand]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah - Chapter 6 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 6 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the eight night visions (vv. 1–8) with four chariots dispatched as divine agents, then shifts to a sign-act in which Zechariah crowns Joshua the high priest and delivers the “Branch” oracle (vv. 9–15).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The Branch

The title “Branch” is a messianic designation for a coming king who will build the temple and unite kingship and priesthood on one throne, with “counsel of peace” between the two offices (vv. 12–13).

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Nested Quotations

Verses 10–15 contain three levels of quotation as Yahweh instructs Zechariah to speak to Joshua a message from Yahweh of Armies.

title: Zechariah - Chapter 6 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 6 General Notes

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written mainly in prose and tells the last vision of the four chariots in the first part of the chapter.

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetic song in 6:12–13.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Meaning of the visions

The visions are stated and even when the prophet asked for an explanation, their true meaning is often obscure. This uncertainty should remain in your translation. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

title: Zechariah 6:1 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אָשֻׁ֗ב

"And I turned"

Zechariah is using the phrase translated as And I turned to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 6:1 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֤א עֵינַ⁠י֙

"and I lifted my eyes"

Zechariah is using I lifted my eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “I looked up.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I looked up]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 6:1 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֨ה

"and behold"

Zechariah is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 6:1 (#4)
content:
אַרְבַּ֤ע מַרְכָּבוֹת֙ יֹֽצְא֔וֹת מִ⁠בֵּ֖ין שְׁנֵ֣י הֶֽ⁠הָרִ֑ים

"four chariots coming out from between two mountains"

Here, four chariots coming out from between two mountains represents the divine agents that Yahweh sends out to execute his purposes in the earth. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote. Alternate translation: [four chariots, which represent the divine agents Yahweh sends out to carry out his purposes, coming out from between two mountains]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Zechariah 6:1 (#5)
content:
הָרֵ֥י נְחֹֽשֶׁת

"were} mountains of bronze"

Here, mountains of bronze represents the permanence and strength of Yahweh’s heavenly dwelling place. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote. Alternate translation: [represented the permanence and strength of Yahweh’s heavenly dwelling place]

See: Symbolic Language

title: Zechariah 6:2 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠מֶּרְכָּבָ֥ה הָ⁠רִֽאשֹׁנָ֖ה & וּ⁠בַ⁠מֶּרְכָּבָ֥ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֖ית

"In the first chariot & and in the second chariot"

If your language would not represent numbers in a form such as first and second, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the chariot that went at the front … and in the chariot that went after it]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Zechariah 6:3 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בַ⁠מֶּרְכָּבָ֥ה הַ⁠שְּׁלִשִׁ֖ית & וּ⁠בַ⁠מֶּרְכָּבָה֙ הָ⁠רְבִעִ֔ית

"and in the third chariot & and in the fourth chariot"

If your language would not represent numbers in a form such as third and fourth, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and in chariot three … and in the last chariot]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Zechariah 6:4 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אַ֨עַן֙ וָֽ⁠אֹמַ֔ר

"And I answered and said"

The phrase And I answered and said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 6:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֥עַן הַ⁠מַּלְאָ֖ךְ וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֑⁠י

"And the angel answered and said to me"

The phrase answered and said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 6:5 (#2)
content:
אַרְבַּע֙ רֻח֣וֹת הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם

"the four winds of the heavens"

Here the angel is speaking as if these chariots were the four winds of the heavens meaning that they go in every direction, covering the entire earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [four messengers from heaven who will cover the entire earth]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 6:5 (#3)
content:
אַרְבַּע֙ רֻח֣וֹת

"the four winds of"

The word translated as winds could mean: (1) wind, denoting directions, Alternate translation: [four directions from] (2) spirits. Alternate translation: [four of God’s servants in]

title: Zechariah 6:5 (#4)
content:
מֵֽ⁠הִתְיַצֵּ֖ב עַל

"from standing before"

Here, standing before represents being ready to serve. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from readiness to serve]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 6:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אֲמֻצִּ֣ים

"And the strong ones"

Zechariah is using the adjective strong as a noun to mean a certain kind of horse. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And the strong horses]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 6:7 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אֲמֻצִּ֣ים יָצְא֗וּ וַ⁠יְבַקְשׁוּ֙ לָ⁠לֶ֨כֶת֙ לְ⁠הִתְהַלֵּ֣ך בָּ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וַ⁠יֹּ֕אמֶר לְכ֖וּ הִתְהַלְּכ֣וּ בָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ וַ⁠תִּתְהַלַּ֖כְנָה בָּ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"And the strong ones went out and sought to go to walk about in the earth. And he said, “Go, walk about in the earth.” And they walked about in the earth"

Here, sought to go marks to walk about in the earth as the goal or purpose of went out. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Zechariah 6:7 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠הִתְהַלֵּ֣ך בָּ⁠אָ֔רֶץ & לְכ֖וּ הִתְהַלְּכ֣וּ בָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ וַ⁠תִּתְהַלַּ֖כְנָה בָּ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"to walk about in the earth & Go, walk about in the earth.” And they walked about in the earth"

Zechariah is using to walk about in the earth as a common expression of the culture to mean “to patrol the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to patrol the earth … Go, walk about in the earth … and they walked about in the earth]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 6:7 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֕אמֶר

"And he said"

The pronoun he refers to the angel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the angel said to them]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:7 (#5)
content:
לְכ֖וּ הִתְהַלְּכ֣וּ בָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"Go, walk about in the earth"

The words translated as Go, walk about in the earth are imperatives, but they communicate permission rather than a command. If the imperatives do not communicate permission for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates permission. Alternate translation: [Go ahead and walk about in the earth]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Zechariah 6:7 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠תִּתְהַלַּ֖כְנָה בָּ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"And they walked about in the earth"

The pronoun they refers to the strong horses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the strong ones walked about in the earth]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּזְעֵ֣ק אֹתִ֔⁠י וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלַ֖⁠י לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"And he called out to me and spoke to me, saying"

The phrase And he called out to me and spoke to me, saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent all three terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּזְעֵ֣ק אֹתִ֔⁠י

"And he called out to me"

The pronoun he refers to the angel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the angel called out to me]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#3)
content:
רְאֵ֗ה

"See"

The angel is using the term See to focus Zechariah’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠יּֽוֹצְאִים֙ אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ צָפ֔וֹן

"the ones going out to the land of the north"

The phrase the ones refers to the chariots with their horses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the chariots going out to the land of the north]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#5)
content:
הֵנִ֥יחוּ אֶת־רוּחִ֖⁠י

"have caused my spirit to rest"

The angel is using have caused my spirit to rest as a common expression of the culture to mean “have satisfied my anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have calmed me down]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#6)
content:
אֶת־רוּחִ֖⁠י

"my spirit"

Here, my spirit represents “my anger” or “my wrath.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my wrath]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 6:8 (#7)
content:
אֶת־רוּחִ֖⁠י

"my spirit"

The pronoun my refers to Yahweh, who is speaking through the angel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s spirit]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:9 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֥י דְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה אֵלַ֥⁠י

"And the word of Yahweh came to me"

Zechariah is using the word of Yahweh came to me as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh communicated a message to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh communicated a message to me]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 6:9 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֥י דְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה אֵלַ֥⁠י לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"And the word of Yahweh came to me, saying"

Zechariah is using the phrase And the word of Yahweh came to me to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 6:10 (#1)
content:
לָק֨וֹחַ֙ מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת הַ⁠גּוֹלָ֔ה

"Take from the exiles"

The next verse clarifies that Zechariah is to take silver and gold from the exiles. You could include this information here if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Take silver and gold from the exiles]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 6:10 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠גּוֹלָ֔ה

"the exiles"

The implication is that the exiles refers to people who had returned from exile in Babylon. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the recently returned exiles]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 6:10 (#3)
content:
מֵ⁠חֶלְדַּ֕י & טוֹבִיָּ֖ה & יְדַֽעְיָ֑ה & יֹאשִׁיָּ֣ה & צְפַנְיָ֔ה

"from Heldai & Tobijah & Jedaiah & Josiah & Zephaniah"

These are the names of men. This Josiah is not the same person as King Josiah.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 6:10 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בָאתָ֤ אַתָּה֙ בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֔וּא וּ⁠בָ֗אתָ בֵּ֚ית

"and you, you shall come on that day, and you shall come to the house of"

If the connection between the phrase and you, you shall come on that day and and you shall come to the house of is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and make sure that you yourself certainly go that very day to the house of]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 6:10 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בָאתָ֤ אַתָּה֙

"and you, you shall come"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verb translated as you shall come already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Zechariah himself is the one who will go to Josiah’s house. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you yourself shall come]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:10 (#6)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֖אוּ מִ⁠בָּבֶֽל

"who have come from Babylon"

The pronoun who refers to Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers or restructure the verse to clarify. Alternate translation: [for Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah have come from Babylon]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לָקַחְתָּ֥ כֶֽסֶף־וְ⁠זָהָ֖ב וְ⁠עָשִׂ֣יתָ עֲטָר֑וֹת וְ⁠שַׂמְתָּ֗ בְּ⁠רֹ֛אשׁ יְהוֹשֻׁ֥עַ בֶּן־יְהוֹצָדָ֖ק הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֥ן הַ⁠גָּדֽוֹל

"And you shall take silver and gold, and you shall make crowns, and you shall set {them} on the head of Joshua, the son of Jehozadak, the high priest"

These instructions are to be carried out in sequence: first take the silver and gold, then make crowns, and then place them on Joshua’s head. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [And you shall take silver and gold, and then you shall make crowns, and then you shall set {them} on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest.]

See: Connect — Sequential Time Relationship

title: Zechariah 6:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָשִׂ֣יתָ עֲטָר֑וֹת וְ⁠שַׂמְתָּ֗ בְּ⁠רֹ֛אשׁ יְהוֹשֻׁ֥עַ

"and you shall make crowns, and you shall set {them} on the head of Joshua"

Placing crowns on the head of Joshua the high priest was a symbolic action by which Yahweh showed that a future king-priest figure would come. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

See: Symbolic Action

title: Zechariah 6:11 (#3)
content:
יְהוֹצָדָ֖ק

"Jehozadak"

Jehozadak is the name of a man, the high priest.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֤ אֵלָי⁠ו֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר

"And you shall speak to him, saying"

The phrase And you shall speak to him, saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, saying"

The phrase Yahweh of Armies, saying introduces a direct quotation within a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent these terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#3)
content:
כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר הִנֵּה־אִ֞ישׁ

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies, saying, Behold, a man"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies says that there is a man]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#4)
content:
הִנֵּה

"Behold"

Yahweh is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#5)
content:
צֶ֤מַח שְׁמ⁠וֹ֙

"Branch is his name"

Here Yahweh is speaking of this future king as if he were a Branch growing from a plant. He means that this person will arise from the line of David. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Descendant is his name]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#6)
content:
הִנֵּה־אִ֞ישׁ צֶ֤מַח שְׁמ⁠וֹ֙

"Behold, a man—Branch is his name"

Here Yahweh is introducing Branch as a new participant in the prophecy. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation.

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#7)
content:
צֶ֤מַח & יִצְמָ֔ח

"Branch & he will sprout"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its subject come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [Branch … he will branch off]

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#8)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠תַּחְתָּ֣י⁠ו יִצְמָ֔ח

"and from his place he will sprout"

Here Yahweh is speaking of this future king as if he were a plant that would sprout from the ground. He means that this person will arise and emerge. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and from his place he will arise]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 6:12 (#9)
content:
וּ⁠בָנָ֖ה אֶת־הֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָֽהּ

"and he will build the temple of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [and he will build my temple]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#1)
content:
וְ֠⁠הוּא יִבְנֶ֞ה

"And he, he will build"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun he separately, even though the verb translated as he will build already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is the Branch who will build the temple of Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And he himself will build the temple of Yahweh]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#2)
content:
אֶת־הֵיכַ֤ל יְהוָה֙

"the temple of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my temple]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֽוּא־יִשָּׂ֣א ה֔וֹד

"and he, he will bear glory"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun he separately, even though the verb translated as he will bear glory already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is this man, the Branch, who will bear glory. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he himself will bear glory]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#4)
content:
יִשָּׂ֣א ה֔וֹד

"he will bear glory"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will be known as great and powerful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֤ה כֹהֵן֙ עַל־כִּסְא֔⁠וֹ

"And he will be a priest on his throne"

This could mean: (1) Branch will be both priest and king or (2) Branch will be king, and another person will be a priest who will share the royal power. Alternate translation: [There will be a priest upon his throne]

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יָשַׁ֥ב וּ⁠מָשַׁ֖ל עַל־כִּסְא֑⁠וֹ

"and he will sit and rule on his throne"

Here, his throne represents “his royal authority.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and will sit and rule with his royal authority]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#7)
content:
וַ⁠עֲצַ֣ת שָׁל֔וֹם

"and a counsel of peace"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of counsel and peace, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and they will advise each other peacefully]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#8)
content:
וַ⁠עֲצַ֣ת שָׁל֔וֹם

"and a counsel of peace"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a counsel that is characterized by peace. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a peaceful counsel]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 6:13 (#9)
content:
בֵּ֥ין שְׁנֵי⁠הֶֽם

"between the two of them"

The implication is that the two of them refers to the offices of king and priest. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [between the two offices of king and priest.’]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 6:14 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠חֵ֨לֶם֙

"for Helem"

The word Helem is the name of a man. This is an alternate form of the name Heldai from verse 10.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 6:14 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠חֵ֖ן בֶּן־צְפַנְיָ֑ה

"and for Hen, the son of Zephaniah"

The word Hen is the name of a man. This is an alternate form of the name Josiah from verse 10.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 6:14 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠זִכָּר֖וֹן

"as a memorial"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of memorial, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that people would remember]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 6:14 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠זִכָּר֖וֹן בְּ⁠הֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָֽה

"as a memorial in the temple of Yahweh"

Storing the crowns in the temple of Yahweh was a symbolic action by which the people showed that Yahweh had promised a future king-priest. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [as a memorial in the temple of Yahweh to show that Yahweh has promised a future king-priest]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Zechariah 6:14 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠הֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָֽה

"in the temple of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [in my temple]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 6:15 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠רְחוֹקִ֣ים

"And those far off"

Yahweh is using the adjective far off as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [People who live far away]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 6:15 (#2)
content:
יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁלָחַ֣⁠נִי אֲלֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh of Armies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh of Armies, sent this messenger to you]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 6:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָה֙ אִם־שָׁמ֣וֹעַ תִּשְׁמְע֔וּ⁠ן בְּ⁠ק֖וֹל יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם

"And {this} will happen if listening, you will listen to the voice of Yahweh your God"

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that these things will only happen if the people obey Yahweh. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [And if you will listen carefully to the voice of Yahweh your God, this will happen]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Zechariah 6:15 (#4)
content:
שָׁמ֣וֹעַ תִּשְׁמְע֔וּ⁠ן

"listening, you will listen"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb listen in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you will certainly listen]

See: Reduplication

title: Zechariah 6:15 (#5)
content:
תִּשְׁמְע֔וּ⁠ן בְּ⁠ק֖וֹל יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם

"you will listen to the voice of Yahweh your God"

Yahweh is using listen to the voice of Yahweh your God as a common expression of the culture to mean “obey what Yahweh your God commands.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will obey Yahweh your God]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 6:15 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠ק֖וֹל יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם

"to the voice of Yahweh your God"

Here, the voice of Yahweh your God represents “the commands of Yahweh your God.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the instructions of Yahweh your God]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah - Chapter 7 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 7 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Zechariah 7 shifts from prophetic visions to prose narrative. A delegation from Bethel asks whether to continue fast in the fifth month, and Yahweh responds with two oracles (vv. 4–7, 8–14) that redirect the question from ritual observance to justice, covenant faithfulness, and mercy.

Chapters 7–8 as a Mirrored Unit

Chapters 7–8 are shaped as a mirrored (chiastic) unit: the opening question about fasting (7:1–3) is answered at the very end (8:18–19); the first sermon on fasting (7:4–14) is balanced by a second sermon (8:9–17), with the covenant sayings (8:1–8) forming the center.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Fasting as Ritual Mourning

The fifth-month fast commemorated the destruction of Solomon’s temple. Yahweh challenges the people as to whether this practice honored him or merely served the people themselves.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Nested Quotation Levels

Verses 5–7 and 9–10 contain three levels of quotation (narrator, Yahweh, inner message), requiring careful management of quotation marking conventions.

title: Zechariah 7:1 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יְהִי֙ בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַרְבַּ֔ע לְ⁠דָרְיָ֖וֶשׁ הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ

"And it happened in the fourth year of Darius the king"

Zechariah is using the word translated as And it happened to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 7:1 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַרְבַּ֔ע לְ⁠דָרְיָ֖וֶשׁ הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ & בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֛ה לַ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הַ⁠תְּשִׁעִ֖י בְּ⁠כִסְלֵֽו

"in the fourth year of Darius the king & on the fourth {day} of the ninth month, in Kislev"

Here Zechariah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Zechariah 7:1 (#3)
content:
הָיָ֨ה דְבַר־יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־זְכַרְיָ֗ה

"the word of Yahweh came to Zechariah"

The name Zechariah refers to the prophet himself, who also narrates this book in the first person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the word of Yahweh came to me, Zechariah]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:1 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֛ה לַ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הַ⁠תְּשִׁעִ֖י

"on the fourth {day} of the ninth month"

If your language would not represent numbers in a form such as fourth and ninth, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on day four of month nine]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Zechariah 7:1 (#5)
content:
לַ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הַ⁠תְּשִׁעִ֖י בְּ⁠כִסְלֵֽו

"of the ninth month, in Kislev"

The Kislev month of the Hebrew calendar includes parts of November and December on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Zechariah 7:2 (#1)
content:
בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל

"Bethel"

Here, Bethel represents the people who lived in that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The people who lived in Bethel]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 7:2 (#2)
content:
שַׂר־אֶ֕צֶר וְ⁠רֶ֥גֶם מֶ֖לֶךְ

"Sharezer and Regem-Melech"

The words Sharezer and Regem-Melech are the names of men.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 7:2 (#3)
content:
וַֽ⁠אֲנָשָׁ֑י⁠ו

"and his men"

The pronoun their refers to Sharezer and Regem-Melech. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the men who were with them]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:2 (#4)
content:
אֶת־פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"before the face of Yahweh"

Here, the face of Yahweh represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the presence of Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 7:3 (#1)
content:
הַֽ⁠אֶבְכֶּה֙ & כַּ⁠מֶּ֥ה

"Should I mourn & many"

The pronoun I refers to the people of Bethel collectively, speaking through their envoys. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Should we mourn in the fifth month by means of a fast, as we have done these many years]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:3 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠בֵית־יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"at the house of Yahweh of Armies"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the temple as if it were a house in which Yahweh lived. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the temple where Yahweh of hosts lives]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 7:3 (#3)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר אֶל־הַ⁠כֹּֽהֲנִים֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ לְ⁠בֵית־יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת וְ⁠אֶל־הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֖ים לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר הַֽ⁠אֶבְכֶּה֙ בַּ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הַ⁠חֲמִשִׁ֔י הִנָּזֵ֕ר כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשִׂ֔יתִי זֶ֖ה כַּ⁠מֶּ֥ה שָׁנִֽים

"saying to the priests who {were} at the house of Yahweh of Armies, {and} to the prophets saying, “Should I mourn in the fifth month by means of a fast, as I have done these many years"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [They asked the priests who were at the house of Yahweh of hosts and the prophets whether they should mourn in the fifth month by means of a fast, as they had done for many years]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 7:5 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר כִּֽי־צַמְתֶּ֨ם

"and say, ‘When you fasted"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and ask them if when you fasted]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 7:5 (#2)
content:
כִּֽי־צַמְתֶּ֨ם וְ⁠סָפ֜וֹד

"When you fasted and mourned"

The word you is plural here because Yahweh is addressing all the people of the land and the priests, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Zechariah 7:5 (#3)
content:
הֲ⁠צ֥וֹם צַמְתֻּ֖⁠נִי אָֽנִי

"were you fasting, fasting for me"

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people for fasting for their own benefit rather than truly honoring him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you were not truly fasting for me.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 7:5 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠צ֥וֹם צַמְתֻּ֖⁠נִי אָֽנִי

"were you fasting, fasting for me"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb fasting in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [were you truly fasting for me]

See: Reduplication

title: Zechariah 7:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כִ֥י תֹאכְל֖וּ וְ⁠כִ֣י תִשְׁתּ֑וּ

"When you ate and when you drank"

The word you is plural here because Yahweh is continuing to address all the people of the land and the priests, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Zechariah 7:6 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֤וֹא אַתֶּם֙ הָ⁠אֹ֣כְלִ֔ים וְ⁠אַתֶּ֖ם הַ⁠שֹּׁתִֽים

"did you not eat and drink for yourselves"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the people were eating and drinking for their own benefit. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you ate and drank only for yourselves.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 7:7 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר קָרָ֤א יְהוָה֙

"Were these not the words that Yahweh proclaimed"

Yahweh is using the question form to remind the people that these are the same messages he gave through the earlier prophets. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [These were the same words that Yahweh proclaimed]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 7:7 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֗ים

"Were these not the words"

The next verse clarifies that the pronoun these refers to the messages about justice and mercy that Yahweh had proclaimed through the earlier prophets. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Were these messages about justice and mercy not the same words that]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:7 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠יַד֙ הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֣ים הָ⁠רִֽאשֹׁנִ֔ים

"by the hand of the former prophets"

Here, by the hand of the former prophets represents the words that the prophets spoke. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by what the former prophets said]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 7:7 (#4)
content:
בִּ⁠הְי֤וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יֹשֶׁ֣בֶת וּ⁠שְׁלֵוָ֔ה וְ⁠עָרֶ֖י⁠הָ סְבִיבֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"when you still inhabited Jerusalem and the surrounding cities in prosperity"

Zechariah is using the clause when you still inhabited Jerusalem and the surrounding cities in prosperity to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for the prophetic messages that Yahweh proclaimed during this time. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [while you were still living in Jerusalem and the surrounding cities in prosperity and were settled in the Negev, and the foothills to the west]

See: Connect — Background Information

title: Zechariah 7:7 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠נֶּ֥גֶב & יֹשֵֽׁב

"and were settled in the Negev"

The expression were settled is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and had settled in the Negev]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 7:8 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יְהִי֙ דְּבַר־יְהוָ֔ה אֶל־זְכַרְיָ֖ה

"The word of Yahweh came to Zechariah"

Zechariah is using the phrase The word of Yahweh came to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies saying"

The word from Yahweh in verses 9–14 are providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#2)
content:
כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר מִשְׁפַּ֤ט אֱמֶת֙ שְׁפֹ֔טוּ

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies saying, ‘Judge with true justice"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies commands you to judge with true justice]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#3)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"saying"

The phrase saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#4)
content:
אֱמֶת֙ שְׁפֹ֔טוּ

"with true justice"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [rightly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠חֶ֣סֶד וְ⁠רַֽחֲמִ֔ים

"and covenant faithfulness, and mercy"

The terms covenant faithfulness and mercy mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and steadfast love]

See: Doublet

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠חֶ֣סֶד

"and covenant faithfulness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of covenant faithfulness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [be faithful to what you agreed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠רַֽחֲמִ֔ים

"and mercy"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of mercy, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and be merciful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#8)
content:
עֲשׂ֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ אֶת־אָחִֽי⁠ו

"Let each man do this for his brother"

Here the masculine terms man and his brother have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Let each person do this for one another]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 7:9 (#9)
content:
אֶת־אָחִֽי⁠ו

"for his brother"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if each fellow Israelite were his brother. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for his fellow Israelite]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 7:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠רָעַת֙

"and & evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and … anything harmful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 7:10 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠לְבַבְ⁠כֶֽם

"in your heart"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if people’s thoughts and intentions were located in their heart. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your thoughts]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 7:11 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְמָאֲנ֣וּ

"But they refused"

The pronoun they refers to the ancestors of the people Yahweh is currently addressing, not to the current audience. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But their ancestors refused]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:11 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּתְּנ֥וּ כָתֵ֖ף סֹרָ֑רֶת

"and gave a stubborn shoulder"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the people as if they were stubborn animals that gave a stubborn shoulder and refused to be led. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and refused to be led or directed]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 7:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אָזְנֵי⁠הֶ֖ם הִכְבִּ֥ידוּ מִ⁠שְּׁמֽוֹעַ

"Their ears were heavy from hearing"

Here Zechariah is speaking as if their ears were heavy so that they could not hear. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Their ears were closed to hearing] or [They would not listen]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 7:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לִבָּ֞⁠ם שָׂ֣מוּ שָׁמִ֗יר

"They made their heart as rock"

The point of this comparison is that just as rock is hard and unyielding, so were the people’s hearts resistant to Yahweh’s commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They hardened their hearts and made them unwilling to obey]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 7:12 (#2)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠תּוֹרָ֤ה

"the law"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the law, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what God commanded]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 7:12 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠יַ֖ד הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֣ים הָ⁠רִֽאשֹׁנִ֑ים

"by the hand of the former prophets"

See how you translated this same phrase in Zechariah 7:7. Alternate translation: [through the words of the prophets]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 7:13 (#1)
content:
קָרָ֖א

"he called"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh called]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:13 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֣א שָׁמֵ֑עוּ כֵּ֤ן יִקְרְאוּ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א אֶשְׁמָ֔ע

"and they did not listen, so when they call, I will not listen"

The first pronoun they refer to the ancestors who refused to listen in the past, the second refers to any future hearers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the ancestors did not listen, so when their descendants call I will not listen]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:13 (#3)
content:
כַ⁠אֲשֶׁר & כֵּ֤ן

"as when & so"

The phrases translated as as when … so indicates that what follows is a result that mirrors what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a consequence of what came before. Alternate translation: [So because when he called, they did not listen, they will call out to me, but I will not answer]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 7:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֣סָעֲרֵ֗⁠ם

"And I scattered them with a whirlwind"

Here Yahweh is speaking of his judgment as if it were a whirlwind that scatters people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For I violently scattered them]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 7:14 (#2)
content:
אַֽחֲרֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"after them"

The pronoun them refers to the Israelites whom Yahweh has scattered. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [after the Israelites are gone]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 7:14 (#3)
content:
מֵֽ⁠עֹבֵ֖ר וּ⁠מִ⁠שָּׁ֑ב

"from anyone passing through or returning"

Yahweh is referring to all human activity in the land by naming two major components, pass through and returning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [For no one will ever be in the land again]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 7:14 (#4)
content:
אֶֽרֶץ־חֶמְדָּ֖ה

"the land of desire"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a land of desire that is characterized by being desirable. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the desirable land]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah - Chapter 8 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 8 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents a series of prophetic oracles introduced by the messenger formula “Thus says Yahweh of Armies” moving from Yahweh’s commitment to Zion (vv. 1–8) through encouragement to rebuild the temple (vv. 9–15), ethical demands (vv. 16–17), and a vision of the nations seeking Yahweh (vv. 18–23).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Fasts Becoming Festivals

The four fast days commemorating Jerusalem’s fall will become joyful celebrations when Yahweh restores his people.

title: Zechariah 8:1 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

The term saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:1 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֛י דְּבַר־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת

"And the word of Yahweh of Armies came"

Zechariah is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 8:2 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase Thus says Yahweh of Armies introduces a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:2 (#2)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת קִנֵּ֥אתִי לְ⁠צִיּ֖וֹן

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies, ‘I have been jealous for Zion"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. In this verse, Zechariah is quoting what Yahweh says directly. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh of hosts, am passionate for Zion]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 8:2 (#3)
content:
קִנֵּ֥אתִי לְ⁠צִיּ֖וֹן קִנְאָ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֑ה וְ⁠חֵמָ֥ה גְדוֹלָ֖ה קִנֵּ֥אתִי לָֽ⁠הּ

"I have been jealous for Zion {with} a great jealousy, and I have been jealous for her {with} great heat"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I have been extremely jealous for Zion with great heat]

See: Parallelism

title: Zechariah 8:2 (#4)
content:
קִנְאָ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֑ה

"with} a great jealousy"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of jealousy, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and desire to keep her as my own]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:2 (#5)
content:
לָֽ⁠הּ

"for her {with"

The pronoun her refers to Zion. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for Zion with]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 8:2 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠חֵמָ֥ה גְדוֹלָ֖ה קִנֵּ֥אתִי לָֽ⁠הּ

"and I have been jealous for her {with} great heat"

Yahweh is speaking of his strong jealousy as if it were heat. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I have been jealous for her with much anger toward her enemies]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה

"Thus says Yahweh"

The phrase Thus says Yahweh introduces a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#2)
content:
כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה שַׁ֚בְתִּי אֶל־צִיּ֔וֹן

"Thus says Yahweh, ‘I will return to Zion"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. In this verse, Zechariah is quoting what Yahweh says directly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will return to Zion]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#3)
content:
יְרֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠נִקְרְאָ֤ה

"and Jerusalem will be called"

The expression Jerusalem will be called is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will call Jerusalem]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הַר־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת

"and the mountain of Yahweh of Armies"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh of Armies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [and my mountain]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#5)
content:
יְרֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠נִקְרְאָ֤ה & עִ֣יר־הָֽ⁠אֱמֶ֔ת

"and Jerusalem will be called “the city of faithfulness"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a city of faithfulness that is characterized by being faithful. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the faithful city]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#6)
content:
הָֽ⁠אֱמֶ֔ת

"faithfulness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of faithfulness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [where people are faithful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠הַר־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת

"and the mountain of Yahweh of Armies"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that the mountain of Yahweh of hosts refers to Mount Zion. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Mount Zion]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#8)
content:
צְבָא֖וֹת הַ֥ר

"Armies, “the mountain of"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Armies will be called “the mountain of]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 8:3 (#9)
content:
הַ֥ר הַ⁠קֹּֽדֶשׁ

"the mountain of holiness"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the mountain of holiness as a mountain that is characterized by holiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the holy mountain]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:4 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:2.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:4 (#2)
content:
זְקֵנִ֣ים וּ⁠זְקֵנ֔וֹת

"Old men and old women"

Yahweh is referring to all elderly people by naming two major components, Old men and old women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The elderly]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 8:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אִ֧ישׁ מִשְׁעַנְתּ֛⁠וֹ בְּ⁠יָד֖⁠וֹ

"and a man {with} his staff in his hand"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and each person with a staff in hand]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 8:4 (#4)
content:
מֵ⁠רֹ֥ב יָמִֽים

"from a multitude of days"

Yahweh is using from a multitude of days as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of old age.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of old age]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 8:5 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠רְחֹב֤וֹת הָ⁠עִיר֙ יִמָּ֣לְא֔וּ יְלָדִ֖ים וִֽ⁠ילָד֑וֹת

"And the open areas of the city will be filled {with} boys and girls"

The expression will be filled is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Boys and girls will fill the open areas of the city,]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 8:5 (#2)
content:
יְלָדִ֖ים וִֽ⁠ילָד֑וֹת

"boys and girls"

Yahweh is referring to all children by naming both major components, boys and girls. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the children]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 8:6 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת

"Thus says Yahweh of Armies"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:2.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:6 (#2)
content:
כִּ֣י יִפָּלֵ֗א

"If it is wonderful"

Yahweh is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what Yahweh is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [Since it is wonderful]

See: Connect — Factual Conditions

title: Zechariah 8:6 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠עֵינֵי֙ שְׁאֵרִית֙ הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה

"in the eyes of the remnant of this people"

Yahweh is using in the eyes of as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the opinion of the remnant of this people]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 8:6 (#4)
content:
גַּם & יִפָּלֵ֔א

"will it also be wonderful"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that nothing is too difficult for him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [it will not be wonderful in my eyes]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Zechariah 8:6 (#5)
content:
נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase declaration of Yahweh of Armies affirms that the preceding words are from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of representing this kind of affirmation in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:7 (#1)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֥י

"Behold"

Yahweh is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look!]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 8:7 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִזְרָ֑ח וּ⁠מֵ⁠אֶ֖רֶץ מְב֥וֹא הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"from the land of the sunrise and from the land of the setting of the sun"

Yahweh is referring to all of the places where his people are scattered by naming two extremes, the land of the sunrise and the land of the setting of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from every country, whether east or west]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 8:8 (#1)
content:
אֶהְיֶ֤ה לָ⁠הֶם֙ לֵֽ⁠אלֹהִ֔ים

"I will be to them as God"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a covenant relationship in which he is the God whom the people worship and serve. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will be the God whom they worship and serve]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 8:8 (#2)
content:
וַֽ⁠אֲנִי֙ אֶהְיֶ֤ה

"and I, I will be"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I will be already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his own commitment to be the God of his people, matching the reciprocal relationship he describes: they will be his people, and he himself will be their God. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and I myself will be]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 8:8 (#3)
content:
בֶּ⁠אֱמֶ֖ת וּ⁠בִ⁠צְדָקָֽה

"in faithfulness and in righteousness"

The phrase in faithfulness and in righteousness expresses a single idea. The word faithfulness tells more about righteousness. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [with faithful righteousness]

See: Hendiadys

title: Zechariah 8:9 (#1)
content:
תֶּחֱזַ֣קְנָה יְדֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"May your hands be strong"

Yahweh is using hands to represent the whole person and their courage to work. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be strong and courageous]

See: Synecdoche

title: Zechariah 8:9 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠שֹּֽׁמְעִים֙ בַּ⁠יָּמִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה אֵ֖ת הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה מִ⁠פִּי֙ הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֔ים אֲ֠שֶׁר בְּ⁠י֞וֹם יֻסַּ֨ד בֵּית־יְהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת

"you who are hearing in these days these words from the mouth of the prophets who {were} there on the day {when} the house of Yahweh of Armies was founded"

This could mean: (1) the message Zechariah is giving today is almost the same as the message that Haggai (probably) gave when the temple construction started. Alternate translation: [you who are hearing today these same words as were from the mouth of the prophets who stood there on the day the house of Yahweh of Armies was founded] (2) prophets had repeatedly given a similar message ever since temple construction had started, these people had been hearing that. Alternate translation: [you who have kept hearing in these days these words from the mouth of the prophets ever since the day the house of Yahweh of Armies was founded]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 8:9 (#3)
content:
יֻסַּ֨ד בֵּית־יְהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת

"the house of Yahweh of Armies was founded"

The expression was founded is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they founded the house of Yahweh of Armies]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 8:9 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠הֵיכָ֖ל לְ⁠הִבָּנֽוֹת

"the temple to be built"

The expression to be built is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [so that they would build the temple]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 8:9 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠פִּי֙ הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֔ים

"from the mouth of the prophets"

Yahweh is using the mouth of the prophets to represent what the prophets said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the prophets]

See: Synecdoche

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#1)
content:
כִּ֗י לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠יָּמִ֣ים הָ⁠הֵ֔ם שְׂכַ֤ר הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ לֹ֣א נִֽהְיָ֔ה וּ⁠שְׂכַ֥ר הַ⁠בְּהֵמָ֖ה אֵינֶ֑⁠נָּה וְ⁠לַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֨א וְ⁠לַ⁠בָּ֤א אֵין־שָׁלוֹם֙ מִן־הַ⁠צָּ֔ר וַ⁠אֲשַׁלַּ֥ח אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם אִ֥ישׁ בְּ⁠רֵעֵֽ⁠הוּ

"For to the face of those days, the wages of man were not, and the wages of the beast, there were none. And for the one going out and for the one coming in there was no peace from the enemy, and I sent every man, each against his neighbor"

Here Yahweh is providing background information to help his listeners understand the contrast he is making. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠יָּמִ֣ים הָ⁠הֵ֔ם

"to the face of those days"

Yahweh is using the expression to the face of to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before those days]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#3)
content:
שְׂכַ֤ר הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙

"the wages of man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the wages of people]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#4)
content:
שְׂכַ֤ר הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ לֹ֣א נִֽהְיָ֔ה וּ⁠שְׂכַ֥ר הַ⁠בְּהֵמָ֖ה אֵינֶ֑⁠נָּה

"the wages of man were not, and the wages of the beast, there were none"

Yahweh is referring to all sources of income by naming two major components, the wages of man and the wages of the beast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [no money could be made in any way]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֨א וְ⁠לַ⁠בָּ֤א

"And for the one going out and for the one coming in"

Yahweh is referring to all of a person’s daily activities by naming two opposites, the one going out and the one coming in. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And for everyone in all their activities]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#6)
content:
שָׁלוֹם֙

"peace"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of peace, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [safety]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:10 (#7)
content:
אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם אִ֥ישׁ בְּ⁠רֵעֵֽ⁠הוּ

"every man, each against his neighbor"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [every person against their neighbor]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 8:11 (#1)
content:
נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:6.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עַתָּ֗ה לֹ֣א כַ⁠יָּמִ֤ים הָ⁠רִֽאשֹׁנִים֙ אֲנִ֔י לִ⁠שְׁאֵרִ֖ית הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת

"But now, I will not be to the remnant of this people like the former days’—the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

Yahweh uses the word But here to indicate a contrast between the former days and the present time. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, now I will not treat the remnant of this people as I did in the former days’—the declaration of Yahweh of Armies.]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 8:12 (#1)
content:
זֶ֣רַע הַ⁠שָּׁל֗וֹם

"there} will be the seed of peace"

Yahweh is speaking of future prosperity as if it were a seed planted in peace that would produce an abundant harvest. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there will be peace and prosperity]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:12 (#2)
content:
כִּֽי

"For"

Here the word For introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Instead]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 8:12 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠שָּׁל֗וֹם

"peace"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:10.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:12 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠גֶּ֜פֶן תִּתֵּ֤ן פִּרְיָ⁠הּ֙ וְ⁠הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ֙ תִּתֵּ֣ן אֶת־יְבוּלָ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֖יִם יִתְּנ֣וּ טַלָּ֑⁠ם

"the vine will give its fruit, and the land will give its produce, and the heavens will give their dew"

Yahweh speaks of the vine, the land, and the heavens as if they were persons who could give things to people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fruit will come from the vine, produce will come from the land, and dew will fall from the heavens]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֡ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ הֱיִיתֶ֨ם קְלָלָ֜ה בַּ⁠גּוֹיִ֗ם בֵּ֤ית יְהוּדָה֙ וּ⁠בֵ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כֵּ֚ן אוֹשִׁ֣יעַ אֶתְ⁠כֶ֔ם וִ⁠הְיִיתֶ֖ם בְּרָכָ֑ה אַל־תִּירָ֖אוּ תֶּחֱזַ֥קְנָה יְדֵי⁠כֶֽם

"And it will be just as you were a curse in the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you and you will be a blessing. Do not fear; let your hands be strong"

The point of this comparison is that just as you were a curse in the nations was certainly true, so it will certainly be true that Yahweh will save them and they will be a blessing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as it was certainly true that you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so it will certainly also be true that I save you and you will be a blessing. Do not fear; let your hands be strong!]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#2)
content:
הֱיִיתֶ֨ם קְלָלָ֜ה בַּ⁠גּוֹיִ֗ם

"you were a curse in the nations"

Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a curse, meaning that other nations would refer to them as an example of what it means to be cursed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the other nations used you as an example of what it means to be cursed]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#3)
content:
קְלָלָ֜ה

"a curse"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of a curse, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of people who were cursed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#4)
content:
בֵּ֤ית יְהוּדָה֙ וּ⁠בֵ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"house of Judah and house of Israel"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So house of Judah figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Judah, and house of Israel means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [people of Judah and people of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#5)
content:
וִ⁠הְיִיתֶ֖ם בְּרָכָ֑ה

"and you will be a blessing"

Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they would actually become a blessing, meaning that other nations would refer to them as an example of what it means to be blessed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will be an example of what it means to be blessed]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#6)
content:
בְּרָכָ֑ה

"a blessing"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of a blessing, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you will be blessed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:13 (#7)
content:
אַל־תִּירָ֖אוּ תֶּחֱזַ֥קְנָה יְדֵי⁠כֶֽם

"Do not fear; let your hands be strong"

Yahweh is using hands to represent the whole person and their courage to work. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be strong and courageous]

See: Synecdoche

title: Zechariah 8:14 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠הָרַ֣ע לָ⁠כֶ֗ם

"to cause harm to you"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of harm, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to harm you]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:14 (#2)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר

"Just as"

Yahweh uses the words Just as and “thus” (next verse) here to indicate a contrast between what he did in the past and what he will do in the future. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language.

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 8:14 (#3)
content:
אָמַ֖ר יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת

"says Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase says Yahweh of Armies is a parenthetical remark that reminds the listener that these are Yahweh’s words. In your translation, use a natural way of representing this kind of attribution in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:15 (#1)
content:
שַׁ֤בְתִּי זָמַ֨מְתִּי֙

"I have turned; I plan"

The words I have turned and I plan express a single idea. The word turned indicates that Yahweh is planning again, reversing his earlier purpose to bring harm. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [I again plan] or [I have decided once more]

See: Hendiadys

title: Zechariah 8:16 (#1)
content:
אֱמֶת֙

"truth"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of truth, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is true]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:16 (#2)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־רֵעֵ֔⁠הוּ

"each with his neighbor"

Here the masculine term his has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [every person with their neighbor]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 8:16 (#3)
content:
שָׁל֔וֹם

"peace"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of peace, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and peaceful resolutions]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:16 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠שַׁעֲרֵי⁠כֶֽם

"in your gates"

Yahweh is using gates to represent the places where legal judgments are made. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your courts]

See: Synecdoche

title: Zechariah 8:16 (#5)
content:
אֱמֶת֙ וּ⁠מִשְׁפַּ֣ט שָׁל֔וֹם שִׁפְט֖וּ בְּ⁠שַׁעֲרֵי⁠כֶֽם

"judge in your gates {with} faithfulness and a judgement of peace"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of faithfulness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [judge in your gates faithfully and peacefully]

title: Zechariah 8:16 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠מִשְׁפַּ֣ט שָׁל֔וֹם

"and a judgement of peace"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of judgement, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and make decisions that bring peace]

title: Zechariah 8:17 (#1)
content:
אֶת־רָעַ֣ת

"evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [do harmful things]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:17 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠לְבַבְ⁠כֶ֔ם

"within his heart"

Here the heart represents where a person’s thoughts and intentions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your thoughts]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 8:17 (#3)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

The phrase the declaration of Yahweh affirms that the preceding words are from Yahweh. This quotation began at verse 2. In your translation, use a natural way of representing this kind of affirmation in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:18 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֛י דְּבַר־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת אֵלַ֥⁠י

"And the word of Yahweh of Armies came to me"

Zechariah is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 8:18 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 8:19 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠שָׂשׂ֣וֹן

"into joy"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of joy, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [joyful times]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:19 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠שָׂשׂ֣וֹן וּ⁠לְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֔ה

"into joy, and into gladness"

The terms joy and gladness mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [times of great joy]

See: Doublet

title: Zechariah 8:19 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֔ה

"and into gladness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of gladness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you gladly celebrate]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:19 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אֱמֶ֥ת

"And & faithfulness"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:16.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:19 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠שָּׁל֖וֹם

"and peace"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:16.

title: Zechariah 8:21 (#1)
content:
אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה

"the face of Yahweh"

Here, the face of Yahweh represents the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the presence of Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 8:21 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר נֵלְכָ֤ה הָלוֹךְ֙ & אֵלְכָ֖ה גַּם־אָֽנִי

"saying, “Let us quickly go & I, I also will go"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. For example, you could translate the direct quotation as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that they should quickly go … And that they themselves would also go]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 8:21 (#3)
content:
אֵלְכָ֖ה גַּם־אָֽנִי

"I, I also will go"

The speaker is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I also will go already includes this meaning. The speaker is doing that to emphasize his own eagerness to join in seeking Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself will also go]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 8:22 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠בַקֵּ֛שׁ אֶת־יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת & וּ⁠לְ⁠חַלּ֖וֹת אֶת־פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"to seek Yahweh of Armies & and beg the face of Yahweh"

See how you translated these same phrases in the previous verse.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 8:23 (#1)
content:
עֲשָׂרָ֣ה אֲנָשִׁ֔ים מִ⁠כֹּ֖ל לְשֹׁנ֣וֹת הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם

"ten men from every language of the nations"

Yahweh is making an extreme statement, saying ten men from every language of the nations, to emphasize the great number of foreigners who will seek to worship him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [countless people from every language and nation]

See: Hyperbole

title: Zechariah 8:23 (#2)
content:
יַחֲזִ֨יקוּ֙ & וְֽ⁠הֶחֱזִ֡יקוּ בִּ⁠כְנַף֩

"will grab, and they will grab the hem of"

To grab the hem of someone’s robe was a symbolic action that expressed a strong desire to accompany that person. If this would not be understood in your culture, you could use a comparable symbolic action from your culture or describe what this action meant.
