Alternate translation: [will beg, they will beg to come along with]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Zechariah 8:23 (#3)
content:
יַחֲזִ֨יקוּ֙ & וְֽ⁠הֶחֱזִ֡יקוּ בִּ⁠כְנַף֩

"will grab, and they will grab the hem of"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb will grab in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [will grab tightly the hem of]

See: Reduplication

title: Zechariah 8:23 (#4)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר נֵֽלְכָה֙ עִמָּ⁠כֶ֔ם כִּ֥י שָׁמַ֖עְנוּ אֱלֹהִ֥ים עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם

"saying, “Let us go with you, for we have heard God is with you"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. For example, you could translate the direct quotation as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that they want to go with him because they have heard that God is with him]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah - Chapter 9 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 9 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophetic oracle (the “burden of the word of Yahweh”) that moves from judgment on the surrounding nations (verses 1–8) to the coming of a righteous, humble king who brings peace (verses 9–10), then to Yahweh’s deliverance and restoration of his people (verses 11–17).

Chapters 9–14 as a Larger Chiasm

Chapters 9–14 are often read as one long, mirrored (chiastic) structure. This chapter’s judgment on the surrounding nations (9:1–8) is balanced at the very end by Yahweh’s kingship over all the earth (14:16–21), while themes of celebration, the rejection of false shepherds, and mourning for the pierced one recur in matching pairs in between.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The blood of the covenant

In verse 11, “the blood of your covenant” refers to the sacrifices that ratified Yahweh’s agreement with Israel, the basis for his freeing his people.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Verse 1

The first verse has several difficulties. The first set centers on Yahweh’s relationship with Hadrach and Damascus. Many English Bibles translate the preposition here (Yahweh “in” the land) as “against’,” but that preposition does not usually have that meaning. It is also not clear what is resting in Damascus. Is it Yahweh or his word or the burden? What does it mean to be his resting place? For the first set, the text and notes will lean toward an interpretation such as “this prophecy is about some place near Hadrach and Damascus; Yahweh is especially present there right now because he is about to do something.” The second set of difficulties centers on the question of whose eyes are looking at whom? Is Yahweh watching the world and Israelites closely? Are the world and the Israelites watching Yahweh closely (as verse 5 may suggest)? Why (beyond translation)? The text and notes will lean toward the interpretation that Yahweh is watching the world closely. This seems to fit with other parts of the book (4:10, 12:4) and verse 8. If a local translation makes a clear decision, you may wish to follow that. Otherwise you may wish to follow the decisions made here.

Shifting speakers and personified cities

The speaker shifts between the prophet and Yahweh (first person), and cities such as Tyre and Ekron are personified as women; track these shifts throughout the chapter.

The Lord

In verse 4 and 14, Yahweh is referred to as “Lord.” While we do not recommend following the custom of translating Yahweh as LORD, if that is the decision your translation has made, you will need to take special care in verse 14 where the text reads “the Lord Yahweh” and follow how you have translated that combination in other places (Ezekiel).

title: Zechariah 9:1 (#1)
content:
מַשָּׂ֤א דְבַר־יְהוָה֙

"The burden of the word of Yahweh"

Zechariah is using the words translated as The burden of the word of Yahweh to introduce a new section of his prophecy. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 9:1 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ

"in the land of"

The word translated as in could mean: (1) concerning. Alternate translation: [about the land of] (2) against. Alternate translation: [against the land of]

title: Zechariah 9:1 (#3)
content:
מְנֻחָת֑⁠וֹ

"his resting place"

The pronoun his could refer to: (1) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s resting place] or (2) the word of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the resting place of Yahweh’s word]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:1 (#4)
content:
כִּ֤י לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עֵ֣ין אָדָ֔ם וְ⁠כֹ֖ל שִׁבְטֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"for toward Yahweh are the eye of mankind and all of the tribes of Israel"

This could mean: (1) Yahweh is attentive to all the world and especially Israel. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s eyes watch all of mankind and all of the tribes of Israel] or (2) everyone in the world, including Israel, are attentive to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [all of mankind and all of the tribes of Israel watch Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:2 (#1)
content:
תִּגְבָּל־בָּ֑⁠הּ

"borders on it"

The pronoun it refers to the land of Hadrach and Damascus. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [borders on the land of Hadrach and Damascus]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:2 (#2)
content:
צֹ֣ר וְ⁠צִיד֔וֹן

"Tyre and Sidon"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [as do Tyre and Sidon]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 9:2 (#3)
content:
צֹ֣ר וְ⁠צִיד֔וֹן כִּ֥י חָֽכְמָ֖ה מְאֹֽד

"Tyre and Sidon, for they are very wise"

Here, they represents the people who live in Tyre and Sidon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Tyre and Sidon, for their inhabitants are very wise]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:2 (#4)
content:
כִּ֥י חָֽכְמָ֖ה מְאֹֽד

"for they are very wise"

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for they consider themselves very wise]

See: Irony

title: Zechariah 9:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּ֥בֶן צֹ֛ר מָצ֖וֹר לָ֑⁠הּ

"And Tyre has built herself a stronghold"

Zechariah is speaking of the city Tyre as if it were a living woman who built herself a stronghold. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people of Tyre have built themselves a stronghold]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 9:3 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּ֥בֶן צֹ֛ר מָצ֖וֹר לָ֑⁠הּ

"And Tyre has built herself a stronghold"

The word herself indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [And Tyre has built a stronghold for her own benefit]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:3 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠תִּצְבָּר־כֶּ֨סֶף֙ כֶּֽ⁠עָפָ֔ר וְ⁠חָר֖וּץ כְּ⁠טִ֥יט חוּצֽוֹת

"and heaped up silver like dust, and refined gold like the mud of the streets"

The point of this comparison is that just as dust and the mud of the streets are extremely common and plentiful, so the silver and refined gold that Tyre accumulated were extremely abundant. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [heaped up silver and refined gold in very great abundance]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֤ה

"Behold"

Behold! The Lord is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#2)
content:
אֲדֹנָ⁠י֙ יֽוֹרִשֶׁ֔⁠נָּה

"The Lord will dispossess her"

The pronoun her refers to the city of Tyre. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The Lord will dispossess Tyre]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִכָּ֥ה בַ⁠יָּ֖ם חֵילָ֑⁠הּ וְ⁠הִ֖יא בָּ⁠אֵ֥שׁ תֵּאָכֵֽל

"and strike down her wealth on the sea, and she, she will be devoured by fire"

Zechariah is speaking of the city of Tyre as if it were a living woman whose wealth could be struck down and who would be devoured by fire. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will destroy the wealth of that city on the sea, and the city will be destroyed by fire]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הִכָּ֥ה & חֵילָ֑⁠הּ

"and strike down her wealth"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wealth, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [strike down all she owns]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הִ֖יא בָּ⁠אֵ֥שׁ תֵּאָכֵֽל

"and she, she will be devoured by fire"

Here, fire represents “destruction in war.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and she will be destroyed in war]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הִ֖יא בָּ⁠אֵ֥שׁ תֵּאָכֵֽל

"and she, she will be devoured by fire"

Zechariah is stating the pronoun she separately, even though the verb translated as will be devoured already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Tyre itself will be destroyed. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Tyre itself will be devoured by fire]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:4 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠הִ֖יא בָּ⁠אֵ֥שׁ תֵּאָכֵֽל

"and she, she will be devoured by fire"

The expression she will be devoured by fire is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and fire will devour her]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 9:5 (#1)
content:
אַשְׁקְל֜וֹן & וְ⁠עַזָּה֙ & וְ⁠עֶקְר֖וֹן

"Ashkelon & and Gaza & and Ekron"

Here, Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron represent the people who live in those cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Ashkelon … and the people of Gaza … And the people of Ekron]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עַזָּה֙ וְ⁠תָחִ֣יל מְאֹ֔ד

"and Gaza, and it will writhe greatly"

Here Zechariah is speaking as if Gaza’s terror were a physical pain that would make the city writhe greatly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Gaza also will be greatly distressed]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:5 (#3)
content:
כִּֽי־הֹבִ֣ישׁ מֶבָּטָ֑⁠הּ

"for her hope has dried up"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of hope, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for she no longer expects good things to happen]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 9:5 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עֶקְר֖וֹן כִּֽי־הֹבִ֣ישׁ מֶבָּטָ֑⁠הּ

"and Ekron, for her hope has dried up"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ekron will also see and tremble, for her hope has dried up]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 9:5 (#5)
content:
הֹבִ֣ישׁ מֶבָּטָ֑⁠הּ

"her hope has dried up"

Here Zechariah is speaking of Ekron’s hope as if it were a stream or spring that has dried up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [she has no more hope]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:5 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠אַשְׁקְל֖וֹן לֹ֥א תֵשֵֽׁב

"and Ashkelon will not be inhabited"

The expression Ashkelon will not be inhabited is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will no longer inhabit Ashkelon]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 9:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֖י גְּא֥וֹן

"and I will cut off the pride of"

The pronoun I refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will cut off the pride]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:6 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֖י גְּא֥וֹן פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים

"and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the pride of the Philistines were something that he could cut off with a blade. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will put an end to the arrogance of the Philistines]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:6 (#3)
content:
גְּא֥וֹן פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים

"the pride of the Philistines"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of pride, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the Philistines are proud of]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 9:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֖י גְּא֥וֹן פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים

"and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines"

Here, the pride of the Philistines represents their mightiness as seen in the glory of their king and their controlling who lives in their own cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will make the Philistines an insignificant people group]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:7 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠הֲסִרֹתִ֨י דָמָ֜י⁠ו מִ⁠פִּ֗י⁠ו וְ⁠שִׁקֻּצָי⁠ו֙ מִ⁠בֵּ֣ין שִׁנָּ֔י⁠ו

"And I will remove his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between his teeth"

Here, his blood and his abominations represent the meat with blood in it and the food sacrificed to idols that the Philistines ate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And I will remove the meat with blood in it from his mouth and the food sacrificed to idols from between his teeth]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:7 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠הֲסִרֹתִ֨י דָמָ֜י⁠ו מִ⁠פִּ֗י⁠ו וְ⁠שִׁקֻּצָי⁠ו֙ מִ⁠בֵּ֣ין שִׁנָּ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠נִשְׁאַ֥ר גַּם־ה֖וּא לֵֽ⁠אלֹהֵ֑י⁠נוּ וְ⁠הָיָה֙ כְּ⁠אַלֻּ֣ף בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֔ה

"And I will remove his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between his teeth, and he also will be left behind for our God, and he will be like a clan in Judah"

The pronouns his and he both refer to the Philistines. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will remove the Philistines’ blood from their mouth and their abominations from between their teeth, and they also will be left behind for our God, and they will be like a clan in Judah]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:7 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָה֙ כְּ⁠אַלֻּ֣ף בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֔ה וְ⁠עֶקְר֖וֹן כִּ⁠יבוּסִֽי

"and he will be like a clan in Judah, and Ekron, like a Jebusite"

The point of these comparisons is that just as a clan in Judah belongs fully to Yahweh’s people, so the surviving Philistines will belong to Yahweh’s people, and just as a Jebusite was absorbed into Israel, so Ekron will be absorbed among them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the surviving Philistines will belong to Yahweh’s people just as a clan in Judah does, and the people of Ekron will be absorbed among them just as the Jebusites were]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:8 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠חָנִ֨יתִי לְ⁠בֵיתִ֤⁠י מִצָּבָה֙ מֵ⁠עֹבֵ֣ר וּ⁠מִ⁠שָּׁ֔ב וְ⁠לֹֽא־יַעֲבֹ֧ר עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם ע֖וֹד נֹגֵ֑שׂ כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה רָאִ֥יתִי בְ⁠עֵינָֽ⁠י

"And I will camp around my house as a guard against the one passing through and against the one returning, and no oppressor will pass over them again, for now I have seen with my eyes"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the last phrase gives the reason for the result that the rest of the verse describes. Alternate translation: [I am paying close attention to what happens to my people like one camping around my house as a guard against the one passing through and against the one returning, and no oppressor will pass over them again.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 9:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠חָנִ֨יתִי לְ⁠בֵיתִ֤⁠י

"And I will camp around my house"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were an army that would camp around his house to protect it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will stand guard around my house]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:8 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בֵיתִ֤⁠י

"around my house"

Here, my house represents his temple and the people connected with it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my temple and those who belong to it]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:8 (#4)
content:
מֵ⁠עֹבֵ֣ר וּ⁠מִ⁠שָּׁ֔ב

"against the one passing through and against the one returning"

Yahweh is using the expressions the one passing through and the one returning as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use such expressions in the same way. If not, you can translate them with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [against enemies who pass through and the enemies who return]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 9:8 (#5)
content:
עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם

"them"

The pronoun them refers to the people connected with Yahweh’s house. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [my people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:8 (#6)
content:
עַתָּ֖ה רָאִ֥יתִי בְ⁠עֵינָֽ⁠י

"now I have seen with my eyes"

Here, now I have seen with my eyes represents “I have begun to pay close attention to and care for my people.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [now I have begun to care for my people]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:9 (#1)
content:
גִּילִ֨י מְאֹ֜ד בַּת־צִיּ֗וֹן הָרִ֨יעִי֙ בַּ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם

"Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem"

The two clauses Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion and Shout, daughter of Jerusalem mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Rejoice with great joy, people of Zion and Jerusalem!]

See: Parallelism

title: Zechariah 9:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נוֹשָׁ֖ע ה֑וּא

"and being saved is he"

The expression being saved is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God saves him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 9:9 (#3)
content:
בַּת־צִיּ֗וֹן & בַּ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם

"daughter of Zion & daughter of Jerusalem"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the people of Jerusalem as if they were a daughter of Zion or daughter of Jerusalem. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of Zion … people of Jerusalem]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:9 (#4)
content:
הִנֵּ֤ה

"Behold"

Zechariah is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 9:9 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠רֹכֵ֣ב עַל־חֲמ֔וֹר וְ⁠עַל־עַ֖יִר בֶּן־אֲתֹנֽוֹת

"and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the son of female donkeys"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. There are not two donkeys. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them. Alternate translation: [and riding on a donkey, even on a young donkey] or [and riding on a donkey’s colt]

See: Parallelism

title: Zechariah 9:9 (#6)
content:
עַ֖יִר בֶּן־אֲתֹנֽוֹת

"a colt, the son of female donkeys"

It might seem that the expression a colt, the son of female donkeys contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [a young donkey]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּי־רֶ֣כֶב מֵ⁠אֶפְרַ֗יִם

"And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim"

The pronoun I refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will cut off the chariot from Ephraim]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּי־רֶ֣כֶב מֵ⁠אֶפְרַ֗יִם וְ⁠סוּס֙ מִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְ⁠נִכְרְתָה֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת מִלְחָמָ֔ה

"And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be cut off"

Here, the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war represents the military power of those regions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will remove all the military power from Ephraim and from Jerusalem]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְרְתָה֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת מִלְחָמָ֔ה

"and the bow of war will be cut off"

The expression the bow of war will be cut off is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will cut off the bow of war]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#4)
content:
קֶ֣שֶׁת מִלְחָמָ֔ה

"the bow of war"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a bow that is characterized by its use in war. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bow used in war]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠דִבֶּ֥ר שָׁל֖וֹם לַ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם

"And he will speak peace to the nations"

Zechariah is using speak peace as a common expression of the culture to mean “proclaim peace.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will make peace with the nations] or [And he will make the nations behave peacefully]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠דִבֶּ֥ר שָׁל֖וֹם לַ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם

"And he will speak peace to the nations"

The pronoun he refers to the king mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king will speak peace to the nations]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#7)
content:
וּ⁠מָשְׁל⁠וֹ֙ מִ⁠יָּ֣ם עַד־יָ֔ם

"and his dominion will be from sea to sea"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dominion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will rule from sea to sea]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 9:10 (#8)
content:
מִ⁠יָּ֣ם עַד־יָ֔ם וּ⁠מִ⁠נָּהָ֖ר עַד־אַפְסֵי־אָֽרֶץ

"will be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth"

Yahweh is referring to all of the earth by naming two major regions, from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [across the entire earth]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 9:11 (#1)
content:
גַּם־אַ֣תְּ

"As for} you also"

Here Zechariah is using the phrase As for you also to introduce the people of Jerusalem as the ones Yahweh now addresses directly. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [As for you also, O Jerusalem]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Zechariah 9:11 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠דַם־בְּרִיתֵ֗⁠ךְ

"by the blood of your covenant"

Here, the blood of your covenant represents the sacrificial blood by which Yahweh confirmed his covenant with the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by the sacrificial blood that sealed my covenant with you]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:11 (#3)
content:
שִׁלַּ֤חְתִּי אֲסִירַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙

"I have set free your prisoners"

The pronoun I refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has set free your prisoners]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:11 (#4)
content:
אֲסִירַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ מִ⁠בּ֔וֹר אֵ֥ין מַ֖יִם בּֽ⁠וֹ

"your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the exile and suffering of the people as if they were prisoners held in a pit in which there is no water. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your captives who are dying in desperate misery]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:12 (#1)
content:
אֲסִירֵ֖י הַ⁠תִּקְוָ֑ה

"prisoners of hope"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of hope, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [prisoners who are hopeful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 9:12 (#2)
content:
שׁ֚וּבוּ לְ⁠בִצָּר֔וֹן אֲסִירֵ֖י הַ⁠תִּקְוָ֑ה

"Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope"

Here Yahweh is speaking of a place of safety and security as if it were a stronghold to which the people could return. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Return to the place where you will be safe, prisoners of hope]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:12 (#3)
content:
מִשְׁנֶ֖ה אָשִׁ֥יב לָֽ⁠ךְ

"that I will return double to you"

Yahweh is using return double to you as a common expression of the culture to mean “restore to you twice as much as you have lost.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I will restore to you twice as much as you have lost]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 9:13 (#1)
content:
כִּֽי

"for"

Here the word for introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [in that]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 9:13 (#2)
content:
בָנַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ צִיּ֔וֹן עַל־בָּנַ֖יִ⁠ךְ יָוָ֑ן

"your sons, Zion, against your sons, Greece"

Yahweh is using your sons, Zion and your sons, Greece as common expressions of the culture to mean the people of Zion and the people of Greece. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Zion against the people of Greece]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 9:13 (#3)
content:
דָרַ֨כְתִּי לִ֜⁠י יְהוּדָ֗ה קֶ֚שֶׁת מִלֵּ֣אתִי אֶפְרַ֔יִם

"I have bent for myself Judah, a bow; I have filled Ephraim"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were a bow that he bends and of Ephraim as the arrow that he uses. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have made the people of Judah like a bow for myself, and I have made the people of Ephraim like arrows]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:13 (#4)
content:
מִלֵּ֣אתִי אֶפְרַ֔יִם

"I have filled Ephraim"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I have filled Ephraim as a quiver of arrows]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 9:13 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֖י⁠ךְ כְּ⁠חֶ֥רֶב גִּבּֽוֹר

"and I will make you like the sword of a mighty man"

The point of this comparison is that just as the sword of a mighty man is powerful and effective in battle, so Yahweh will make his people powerful against their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I will make you very powerful in battle]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:14 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֣ם יֵֽרָאֶ֔ה

"And Yahweh will appear over them"

The pronoun them refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will appear over his people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יָצָ֥א כַ⁠בָּרָ֖ק חִצּ֑⁠וֹ

"and his arrow will go out like the lightning"

The point of this comparison is that just as the lightning flashes suddenly and strikes powerfully, so Yahweh’s arrow will strike his enemies swiftly and powerfully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his arrow will go out suddenly and strike powerfully]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:14 (#3)
content:
וַֽ⁠אדֹנָ֤⁠י יְהֹוִה֙ בַּ⁠שּׁוֹפָ֣ר יִתְקָ֔ע וְ⁠הָלַ֖ךְ בְּ⁠סַעֲר֥וֹת תֵּימָֽן

"and the Lord Yahweh will blow on the shofar and will go with the storms of the south"

Zechariah is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a warrior. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the Lord Yahweh will blow on the trumpet and advance furiously, like a mighty warrior]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:15 (#1)
content:
יְהוָ֣ה צְבָאוֹת֮ יָגֵ֣ן עֲלֵי⁠הֶם֒

"Yahweh of Armies will defend them"

The pronoun them refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies will defend his people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָכְל֗וּ וְ⁠כָֽבְשׁוּ֙ אַבְנֵי־קֶ֔לַע

"and they will devour and will subdue the stones of the sling"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the people utterly defeating their enemies as if they would devour them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will completely defeat and will subdue those who attack them]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁת֥וּ הָמ֖וּ כְּמוֹ־יָ֑יִן

"and they will drink and roar as with wine"

The point of this comparison is that just as men who have drunk wine become loud and boisterous, so the people will drink and roar in their triumph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they will drink and roar in triumph just as drunk men roar]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:15 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠מָֽלְאוּ֙ כַּ⁠מִּזְרָ֔ק כְּ⁠זָוִיּ֖וֹת מִזְבֵּֽחַ

"and they will be full like the bowl, like the corners of the altar"

The point of this comparison is that just as the bowl and the corners of the altar were filled with sacrificial blood, so the people will be full. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they will be as full as the bowl and the corners of the altar are filled with sacrificial blood]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:16 (#1)
content:
וְֽ⁠הוֹשִׁיעָ֞⁠ם יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠הֶ֛ם

"And Yahweh their God will save them"

The pronouns their and them refer to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh the God of his people will save his people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:16 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠ה֖וּא

"on that day"

Zechariah is using the term day to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See the Introduction to Zechariah for a discussion of the phrase “in that day.”

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 9:16 (#3)
content:
כִּ֚י אַבְנֵי־נֵ֔זֶר

"for they are the stones of a crown"

The pronoun they refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for his people are the stones of a crown]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:16 (#4)
content:
כְּ⁠צֹ֣אן עַמּ֑⁠וֹ

"like the flock of his people"

The point of this comparison is that just as a shepherd rescues and protects the flock of his people, so Yahweh will save and care for his people on that day. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as a shepherd saves his sheep]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 9:16 (#5)
content:
כִּ֚י

"for"

Here the word for introduces not a reason but an expansion. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [indeed to him]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 9:16 (#6)
content:
כִּ֚י אַבְנֵי־נֵ֔זֶר מִֽתְנוֹסְס֖וֹת עַל־אַדְמָתֽ⁠וֹ

"for they are the stones of a crown gleaming over his land"

Here Zechariah is speaking of Yahweh’s people as if they were the stones of a crown that sparkle beautifully. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are precious to him and glorious over his land]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 9:17 (#1)
content:
כִּ֥י מַה־טּוּב֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠מַה־יָפְי֑⁠וֹ

"For how {is} his goodness, and how {is} his beauty"

Zechariah is using phrases that express a strong feeling of admiration and praise. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Everything is amazing and wonderful]

See: Exclamations

title: Zechariah 9:17 (#2)
content:
מַה־טּוּב֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠מַה־יָפְי֑⁠וֹ

"how {is} his goodness, and how {is} his beauty"

The pronoun his could refer to: (1) the people. Alternate translation: [how good and beautiful every one is] or (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [how great is Yahweh’s goodness, and how great is Yahweh’s beauty] It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 9:17 (#3)
content:
מַה־טּוּב֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠מַה־יָפְי֑⁠וֹ

"how {is} his goodness, and how {is} his beauty"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of goodness and beauty, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how good he is, and how beautiful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 9:17 (#4)
content:
דָּגָן֙ בַּֽחוּרִ֔ים וְ⁠תִיר֖וֹשׁ יְנוֹבֵ֥ב בְּתֻלֽוֹת

"Grain the young men, and new wine will make the virgins flourish"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine will make the virgins flourish]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah - Chapter 10 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 10 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This prophetic poem first contrasts Yahweh, who gives rain and guidance, with worthless idols and diviners (verses 1–2), then becomes a first-person divine promise to strengthen and regather his scattered people (verses 3–12).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Shepherds and leaders

The shepherds and male goats represent the people’s leaders, while Yahweh is the true shepherd who cares for his flock.

Regathering the exiles

Yahweh promises to bring the house of Judah and the house of Joseph (Ephraim, the northern kingdom) back from Egypt, Assyria, and distant lands.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Shifts in speaker

The chapter alternates between describing Yahweh and Yahweh speaking as “I,” and in verse 11 the referent of “he” is ambiguous. Keep these referents clear.

title: Zechariah 10:1 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠אִ֖ישׁ עֵ֥שֶׂב בַּ⁠שָּׂדֶֽה

"to a man, vegetation in the field"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to a man he gives vegetation in the field]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 10:1 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠אִ֖ישׁ

"to a man"

Zechariah is not referring to a specific man. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to each person]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#1)
content:
כִּ֧י

"For"

The word For introduces the reason Zechariah gives for the command to ask Yahweh for rain rather than trusting in idols and diviners. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason.

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠תְּרָפִ֣ים דִּבְּרוּ־אָ֗וֶן

"household idols speak iniquity"

Since household idols cannot speak, this represents the false messengers that claim to speak for the household idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the false prophets who profess to speak for your silent household idols speak iniquity]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#3)
content:
דִּבְּרוּ־אָ֗וֶן

"speak iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [speak wicked things]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#4)
content:
וַֽ⁠חֲלֹמוֹת֙ הַ⁠שָּׁ֣וא יְדַבֵּ֔רוּ

"and they speak dreams of emptiness"

Zechariah is using the possessive form to describe dreams that are characterized by the emptiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they claim to have visions from their gods but they are just making things up]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#5)
content:
הֶ֖בֶל

"with vanity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of vanity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [worthlessly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#6)
content:
נָסְע֣וּ כְמוֹ־צֹ֔אן יַעֲנ֖וּ כִּֽי־אֵ֥ין רֹעֶֽה

"they journey like a flock; they are afflicted because there is no shepherd"

The point of this comparison is that just as a flock with no shepherd wanders and suffers, so do the people who rely on idols and diviners. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they wander and suffer just as a flock wanders and suffers when there is no shepherd to guide them]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#7)
content:
נָסְע֣וּ כְמוֹ־צֹ֔אן

"they journey like a flock"

The pronoun they refers to the people, not to the idols or the diviners just mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people journey like a flock]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 10:2 (#8)
content:
אֵ֥ין רֹעֶֽה

"there is no shepherd"

Here Zechariah is speaking as if a leader who guides and protects people were a shepherd. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is no leader to guide and protect them]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#1)
content:
עַל־הָֽ⁠רֹעִים֙ חָרָ֣ה אַפִּ֔⁠י

"Against the shepherds my nose burns"

Here Yahweh begins to speak, but there is no verb introducing his words as a quotation. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says, “Against the shepherds my nose burns]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#2)
content:
עַל־הָֽ⁠רֹעִים֙ חָרָ֣ה אַפִּ֔⁠י וְ⁠עַל־הָ⁠עַתּוּדִ֖ים אֶפְק֑וֹד

"Against the shepherds my nose burns, and on the male goats I will attend"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I am furious with the shepherds who lead my people, and I will certainly deal with those leaders]

See: Parallelism

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#3)
content:
הָֽ⁠רֹעִים֙

"the shepherds"

Yahweh is speaking of the leaders of the people as if they were the shepherds of a flock. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Some interpreters think these refer to the foreign leaders (see 11:3). Alternate translation: [the leaders who should be like shepherds]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#4)
content:
חָרָ֣ה אַפִּ֔⁠י

"my nose burns"

Here, **nose ** represents Yahweh’s anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I am furious]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#5)
content:
הָ⁠עַתּוּדִ֖ים

"the male goats"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the corrupt leaders of Judah as if they were the male goats who lead a flock. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the head goats of the flock] or [the leaders]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#6)
content:
חָרָ֣ה אַפִּ֔⁠י

"my nose burns"

Here Yahweh is speaking of his anger as if it were a fire when he says that it burns. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my anger is intense]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#7)
content:
כִּֽי

"For"

The word For introduces the reason for what Yahweh has just said about punishing the leaders: he cares for his people and will restore them. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason.

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#8)
content:
כִּֽי־פָקַד֩ יְהוָ֨ה צְבָא֤וֹת אֶת־עֶדְר⁠וֹ֙

"For Yahweh of Armies attends to his flock"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh of Armies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [For I, Yahweh of Armies, attend to my flock, the house of Judah, and I will make them]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#9)
content:
אֶת־עֶדְר⁠וֹ֙

"his flock"

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were his flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his people]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#10)
content:
אֶת־בֵּ֣ית יְהוּדָ֔ה

"the house of Judah"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of the kingdom of Judah as if they were a single house, or household. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of the kingdom of Judah]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#11)
content:
כְּ⁠ס֥וּס הוֹד֖⁠וֹ

"like a horse of his splendor"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of splendor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like his splendid horse]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 10:3 (#12)
content:
כְּ⁠ס֥וּס הוֹד֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠מִּלְחָמָֽה

"like a horse of his splendor in the battle"

The point of this comparison is that just as the horse of his splendor is strong and majestic in the battle, so the people of Judah will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as strong and majestic in the battle as his splendid warhorse]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:4 (#1)
content:
מִמֶּ֤⁠נּוּ פִנָּה֙

"From him a cornerstone"

The pronoun him refers to Judah, mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [From him, that is, Judah, a cornerstone]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 10:4 (#2)
content:
מִמֶּ֤⁠נּוּ פִנָּה֙

"From him a cornerstone"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to move will come forth from the end of the verse to here at the start. Alternate translation: [From him will come forth a cornerstone]

See: Information Structure

title: Zechariah 10:4 (#3)
content:
פִנָּה֙ & יָתֵ֔ד & קֶ֣שֶׁת מִלְחָמָ֑ה

"a cornerstone & a {tent} peg & a bow of war"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the rulers who will come from Judah as if they were a cornerstone of a building, the tent peg, and a bow of war. Your language may have comparable expressions that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will come forth the ruler who supports them … the ruler who holds them together … the ruler who leads them in war]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָי֨וּ כְ⁠גִבֹּרִ֜ים

"And they will be like warriors"

The pronoun they refers to the people of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Judah will be like warriors]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 10:5 (#2)
content:
כְ⁠גִבֹּרִ֜ים

"like warriors"

The point of this comparison is that just as warriors are strong and victorious in battle, so will the people of Judah be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [strong and victorious like warriors]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:5 (#3)
content:
בּוֹסִ֨ים בְּ⁠טִ֤יט חוּצוֹת֙ בַּ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֔ה

"trampling in the mud of the streets in the battle"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The meaning may be that the warriors will trample their enemies into the mud of the streets. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [trampling their enemies in the mud of the streets in the battle]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 10:5 (#4)
content:
כִּ֥י

"for"

The word for introduces the reason the people of Judah will prevail in battle: Yahweh is with them. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason.

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 10:5 (#5)
content:
יְהוָ֖ה עִמָּ֑⁠ם

"Yahweh is with them"

By Yahweh is with them, Zechariah means that Yahweh will help them win the battle against their enemies. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will help them]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 10:5 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הֹבִ֖ישׁוּ רֹכְבֵ֥י סוּסִֽים

"and they will put to shame the riders of horses"

Here, the expression put to shame represents defeating them in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they will defeat the riders of horses]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 10:6 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י

"for"

The word for introduces the reason Yahweh will restore his people: he has compassion on them. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason.

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 10:6 (#2)
content:
רִֽחַמְתִּ֔י⁠ם

"I have compassion on them"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of compassion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I feel compassionate toward them]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 10:6 (#3)
content:
אֶת־בֵּ֣ית יְהוּדָ֗ה & בֵּ֤ית יוֹסֵף֙

"the house of Judah & the house of Joseph"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Judah and the house of Joseph figuratively mean all the people descended from Judah and from Joseph. Alternate translation: [the people of Judah … the people of Joseph]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָי֤וּ כְ⁠גִבּוֹר֙ אֶפְרַ֔יִם וְ⁠שָׂמַ֥ח לִבָּ֖⁠ם

"And Ephraim will be like a warrior, and their heart will be glad"

The word their is plural, but it refers back to Ephraim, which is grammatically singular. Here the singular name Ephraim stands for all the people of that tribe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Ephraim will be like a warrior, and their heart will be glad]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָי֤וּ כְ⁠גִבּוֹר֙ אֶפְרַ֔יִם

"And Ephraim will be like a warrior"

The point of this comparison is that just as a warrior is strong and courageous, so the people of Ephraim will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And Ephraim will be as strong and courageous as a warrior]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#3)
content:
לִבָּ֖⁠ם

"their heart"

Here the heart represents where a person’s feelings exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their feelings]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#4)
content:
כְּמוֹ־יָ֑יִן

"as {with} wine"

The point of this comparison is that just as wine makes a person feel glad and cheerful, so their hearts will be glad. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as people become cheerful from drinking wine]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠שָׂמַ֥ח לִבָּ֖⁠ם כְּמוֹ־יָ֑יִן

"and their heart will be glad as {with} wine"

The point of this comparison is that just as a person who drinks wine becomes cheerful, so the people of Ephraim will be glad. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [their heart will be glad, just as a person who drinks wine becomes cheerful]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#6)
content:
כְ⁠גִבּוֹר֙

"like a warrior"

The point of this comparison is that just as a warrior is strong and mighty, so Ephraim will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a strong and mighty warrior]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠שָׂמַ֥ח לִבָּ֖⁠ם

"and their heart will be glad"

In this verse, the word heart is singular in form, but it refers to all the people of Ephraim as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “heart.” Alternate translation: [and their hearts will be glad]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Zechariah 10:7 (#8)
content:
יָגֵ֥ל לִבָּ֖⁠ם

"their heart will exult"

Here Zechariah is speaking as if a person’s heart were where their feelings exist. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their feelings will exult]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:8 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י

"for"

Here the word For introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [after all]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 10:8 (#2)
content:
אֶשְׁרְקָ֥ה לָ⁠הֶ֛ם

"I will whistle for them"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were a shepherd who could whistle for his flock to gather them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will summon them]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶזְרָעֵ⁠ם֙ בָּֽ⁠עַמִּ֔ים

"And I will sow them among the peoples"

Here Yahweh is speaking of scattering his people among the nations as if he were planting seed when he says that he will sow them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause them to live among different nations]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠הֲשִֽׁיבוֹתִי⁠ם֙ מֵ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם וּ⁠מֵֽ⁠אַשּׁ֖וּר אֲקַבְּצֵ֑⁠ם

"And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt, and from Assyria I will gather them"

Yahweh is referring to all the places from which he will bring his people back by naming two extremes, the land of Egypt and Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will bring them back from every land, including Egypt and Assyria]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 10:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִמָּצֵ֖א לָ⁠הֶֽם

"and {room} will not be found for them"

The expression will not be found is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will not have enough room]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָבַ֨ר בַּ⁠יָּ֜ם צָרָ֗ה וְ⁠הִכָּ֤ה בַ⁠יָּם֙ גַּלִּ֔ים וְ⁠הֹבִ֕ישׁוּ כֹּ֖ל מְצוּל֣וֹת יְאֹ֑ר

"And he will pass through the sea {of} distress, and he will strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the Nile will dry up"

By he will pass through the sea of distress, and he will strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the Nile will dry up, Zechariah means that Yahweh will remove every danger and obstacle blocking his people’s return to their land, just as he dried up the sea and the Jordan for their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt and into the land. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will clear away every danger that threatens his people, just as he dried up the sea and the Jordan for their ancestors]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יָּ֜ם צָרָ֗ה

"the sea {of} distress"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the troubles his people face as if they were a dangerous sea when he refers to the sea of distress. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the distress that is like a dangerous sea]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עָבַ֨ר בַּ⁠יָּ֜ם

"And he will pass through the sea"

The pronoun he could refer to: (1) Yahweh. In the surrounding verses, Yahweh speaks of himself in the first person, but here he is referred to in the third person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will pass through the sea] or (2) Ephraim, that is the people of the northern tribes of Israel. However, in the surrounding verse Ephraim is always referred to using plural pronouns and verbs. Alternate translation: [And Ephraim will pass through the sea]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠יָּ֜ם צָרָ֗ה

"the sea {of} distress"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of distress, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the distressing sea]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הִכָּ֤ה בַ⁠יָּם֙ גַּלִּ֔ים

"and he will strike the waves in the sea"

Here Yahweh is using the phrase strike the waves in the sea as a common expression to mean that he will subdue the raging waters and overcome the troubles they represent. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will subdue the raging waves in the sea]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הוּרַד֙ גְּא֣וֹן אַשּׁ֔וּר

"And the pride of Assyria will be brought down"

The expression will be brought down is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will bring down the pride of Assyria]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠הוּרַד֙ גְּא֣וֹן אַשּׁ֔וּר

"And the pride of Assyria will be brought down"

Here, the term pride represents the proud nation of Assyria and its army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the proud army of Assyria will be brought down]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 10:11 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠שֵׁ֥בֶט מִצְרַ֖יִם יָסֽוּר

"and the scepter of Egypt will depart"

Here, the term scepter represents the royal power of Egypt, since a scepter is a symbol that a king holds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the royal power of Egypt will be no more]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 10:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠גִבַּרְתִּי⁠ם֙ בַּֽ⁠יהוָ֔ה

"And I will strengthen them in Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [And I will strengthen them in myself, and in my name they will walk]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 10:12 (#2)
content:
יִתְהַלָּ֑כוּ

"they will walk"

Here Yahweh is speaking of how the people will live as if they would walk along a path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will conduct their lives]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 10:12 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בִ⁠שְׁמ֖⁠וֹ

"and in his name"

Here, his name represents Yahweh’s authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and by his authority]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 10:12 (#4)
content:
נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָֽה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Zechariah is using the phrase the declaration of Yahweh to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah - Chapter 11 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 11 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

The chapter opens with a poetic taunt of judgment (verses 1–3), moves to a prophetic sign-act in which Zechariah acts as a shepherd (verses 4–14), and closes with a woe oracle against a worthless shepherd (verses 15–17). The ULT sets verses 1–3 and 17 as poetry.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Shepherds and the flock

Throughout the chapter, the shepherd represents a ruler, and the flock represents the people he leads.

The two staffs

Zechariah names two shepherd’s staffs “Favor” and “Union;” breaking them signifies the ending of Yahweh’s covenant and of the unity between Judah and Israel.

title: Zechariah 11:1 (#1)
content:
פְּתַ֥ח לְבָנ֖וֹן דְּלָתֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"Open your doors, Lebanon"

Zechariah is speaking to Lebanon, a place that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the coming destruction of the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Lebanon. Alternate translation: [People of Lebanon, open your doors]

See: Apostrophe

title: Zechariah 11:1 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠תֹאכַ֥ל אֵ֖שׁ בַּ⁠אֲרָזֶֽי⁠ךָ

"that fire may devour among your cedars"

Zechariah is speaking of fire as if it were a living thing that could devour the trees. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that fire may burn up your cedars]

See: Personification

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#1)
content:
הֵילֵ֤ל & הֵילִ֨ילוּ֙

"Wail & Wail"

The word translated as wail copies the sound of crying or howling. Zechariah uses this word here, and a similar word about lions in verse 3, to make the scene sound sad and urgent, like people weeping and lions roaring. If your language has a word that sounds like crying, use it here. If not, choose words that still sound emotional and urgent, not calm or formal.

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#2)
content:
בְּרוֹשׁ֙

"cypress"

The word cypress refers to a tall evergreen tree, but its exact identification is uncertain; other translations render it as “fir,” “pine,” or “juniper.” If your readers would not be familiar with this kind of tree, you could use the name of a similar tall, valuable evergreen tree that they would recognize, or you could use a more general term, such as “large evergreen tree.” Alternate translation: [fir tree] or [pine tree]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#3)
content:
הֵילֵ֤ל בְּרוֹשׁ֙

"Wail, cypress"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the cypress trees as if they were a person who could wail. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Cry out, cypress, like a mourner] or [Cypress, be greatly distressed]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#4)
content:
הֵילֵ֤ל בְּרוֹשׁ֙ כִּֽי־נָ֣פַל אֶ֔רֶז אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַדִּרִ֖ים שֻׁדָּ֑דוּ הֵילִ֨ילוּ֙ אַלּוֹנֵ֣י בָשָׁ֔ן כִּ֥י יָרַ֖ד יַ֥עַר ה⁠בצור

"Wail, cypress, for the cedar has fallen, because the majestic ones have been devastated! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the fortified forest has gone down"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because the cedar has fallen, wail, cypress, since the majestic ones have been devastated! Because the fortified forest has gone down, wail, oaks of Bashan]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#5)
content:
נָ֣פַל אֶ֔רֶז

"the cedar has fallen"

Zechariah is speaking of powerful rulers as if they were a cedar tree that had fallen. A cedar was one of the tallest, strongest trees in that area, so a fallen cedar pictures a powerful ruler who has lost his power. The text does not say exactly which ruler or nation this is, so keep your translation general instead of naming a specific person or place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the powerful rulers have been overthrown]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#6)
content:
אַדִּרִ֖ים שֻׁדָּ֑דוּ

"the majestic ones have been devastated"

The expression have been devastated is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies have devastated the majestic ones]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 11:2 (#7)
content:
יַ֥עַר ה⁠בצור

"the fortified forest"

The word translated as fortified has a similar spelling to the word for vintage/grape harvest. Some ancient manuscripts and versions read this as “the forest of the vintage,” apparently confusing the two similar words. The ULT and UST follow the reading “the fortified forest” (i.e., an inaccessible or lofty forest), which matches the word form actually present here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [the forest of the vintage has come down]

See: Textual Variants

title: Zechariah 11:3 (#1)
content:
ק֚וֹל יִֽלְלַ֣ת הָ⁠רֹעִ֔ים כִּ֥י שֻׁדְּדָ֖ה אַדַּרְתָּ֑⁠ם ק֚וֹל שַׁאֲגַ֣ת כְּפִירִ֔ים כִּ֥י שֻׁדַּ֖ד גְּא֥וֹן הַ⁠יַּרְדֵּֽן

"The voice of the wailing of the shepherds, for their glory is devastated! The voice of the roaring of the young lions, for the pride of the Jordan is devastated"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The word for glory here is a lot like the word for the “majestic ones” in verse 2. Zechariah repeats this idea to show that everything great and important, both the leaders and the land, has been completely ruined. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen to the shepherds wailing and the young lions roaring, for everything of value to them has been utterly devastated]

See: Parallelism

title: Zechariah 11:3 (#2)
content:
יִֽלְלַ֣ת הָ⁠רֹעִ֔ים & שַׁאֲגַ֣ת כְּפִירִ֔ים

"the wailing of the shepherds & the roaring of the young lions"

Zechariah is speaking of the rulers of the land as if they were shepherds and young lions that were wailing and roaring over what they had lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the crying of the rulers … the mourning of the powerful men]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:3 (#3)
content:
גְּא֥וֹן הַ⁠יַּרְדֵּֽן

"the pride of the Jordan"

Zechariah is using the pride of the Jordan as a common expression of the culture to mean the dense thickets of trees and bushes that grow along the Jordan River. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the dense thickets along the Jordan River are devastated]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 11:4 (#1)
content:
רְעֵ֖ה

"Shepherd"

Yahweh is speaking of leading and caring for the people as if that task were to Shepherd a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take care of]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:4 (#2)
content:
אֶת־צֹ֥אן הַ⁠הֲרֵגָֽה

"the flock of slaughter"

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who are marked for slaughter]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:5 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֨ר קֹנֵי⁠הֶ֤ן יַֽהֲרְגֻ⁠ן֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יֶאְשָׁ֔מוּ וּ⁠מֹכְרֵי⁠הֶ֣ן יֹאמַ֔ר

"which the buyers kill and are not held guilty, and the ones selling them say"

Here Yahweh is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Zechariah 11:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֣א יֶאְשָׁ֔מוּ

"and are not held guilty"

The expression are not held guilty is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one considers them guilty]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 11:5 (#3)
content:
יֹאמַ֔ר בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֖ה וַ⁠אעְשִׁ֑ר

"say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I have become rich"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [say that Yahweh has blessed them, for they have become rich!]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 11:6 (#1)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Even though Yahweh is speaking, he refers to himself in the third person, using the declaration of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [the declaration that I, Yahweh, am making]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Zechariah 11:6 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of declaration, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this is what Yahweh declares]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 11:6 (#3)
content:
אָנֹכִ֜י מַמְצִ֣יא אֶת־הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם אִ֤ישׁ בְּ⁠יַד־רֵעֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ וּ⁠בְ⁠יַ֣ד מַלְכּ֔⁠וֹ

"I am causing mankind to fall, each man, in the hand of his neighbor and in the hand of his king"

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were causing people to fall into the power of their neighbors and king, as though pushing them down so that others could seize them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am handing mankind over, each man, to his neighbor and to his king]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:6 (#4)
content:
אֶת־הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם

"mankind"

Here the masculine terms mankind and each man have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [all people]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 11:6 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠יַד־רֵעֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ וּ⁠בְ⁠יַ֣ד מַלְכּ֔⁠וֹ & מִ⁠יָּדָֽ⁠ם

"in the hand of his neighbor and in the hand of his king & from their hand"

Here, hand represents power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [under the control of his neighbor and of his king … from their power]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 11:7 (#1)
content:
עֲנִיֵּ֣י הַ⁠צֹּ֑אן

"the poor of the flock"

Zechariah is using the adjective poor as a noun to mean a certain kind of sheep. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the suffering sheep of the flock]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 11:7 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠אַחַ֞ד קָרָ֤אתִי נֹ֨עַם֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠אַחַד֙ קָרָ֣אתִי חֹֽבְלִ֔ים

"For the one I called “Favor,” and for the other I called “Union"

The words Favor and Union are names that Zechariah gave to his two shepherd’s staffs. He chose names that carry meaning, since the staffs represent Yahweh’s relationship with the people.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 11:8 (#1)
content:
אֶת־שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת הָ⁠רֹעִ֖ים

"the three shepherds"

The implication is that these three shepherds were leaders of the people whom Yahweh removed from their position. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the three leaders who were poorly shepherding the people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 11:8 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּקְצַ֤ר נַפְשִׁ⁠י֙ בָּ⁠הֶ֔ם

"And my soul became short with them"

Zechariah is using my soul became short with them as a common expression of the culture to mean that he became impatient with them. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I became tired of them]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 11:9 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מֵּתָ֣ה תָמ֗וּת וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּכְחֶ֨דֶת֙ תִּכָּחֵ֔ד

"The one dying, let it die, and the one being destroyed, let it be destroyed"

Zechariah is repeating forms of the verbs die and destroy in order to intensify his expression of the idea that the flock is doomed and beyond saving. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Let the ones who are going to die, die, and let the ones who are going to be destroyed, be destroyed]

See: Reduplication

title: Zechariah 11:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּכְחֶ֨דֶת֙ תִּכָּחֵ֔ד

"and the one being destroyed, let it be destroyed"

The expression let it be destroyed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let the one perishing perish]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 11:9 (#3)
content:
תֹּאכַ֕לְנָה אִשָּׁ֖ה אֶת־בְּשַׂ֥ר רְעוּתָֽ⁠הּ

"let them eat, each one, the flesh of her companion"

Zechariah is speaking of the people as if they were sheep that would eat the flesh of one another. He means mean that they will turn against and destroy one another. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let each one destroy the other]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:10 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶקַּ֤ח אֶת־מַקְלִ⁠י֙ אֶת־נֹ֔עַם וָ⁠אֶגְדַּ֖ע אֹת֑⁠וֹ לְ⁠הָפֵיר֙ אֶת־בְּרִיתִ֔⁠י אֲשֶׁ֥ר כָּרַ֖תִּי אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠עַמִּֽים

"And I took my staff Favor, and I chopped it up, to break my covenant that I had cut with all the peoples"

Here, to marks the words break my covenant that I had cut with all the peoples as the goal or purpose of his chopping up the staff Favor. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Zechariah 11:10 (#2)
content:
אֶת־בְּרִיתִ֔⁠י אֲשֶׁ֥ר כָּרַ֖תִּי

"my covenant that I had cut"

Zechariah is using the word cut as a common expression of the culture to mean “make,” since in that culture people spoke of making a covenant as cutting it. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my covenant that I had made]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 11:10 (#3)
content:
כָּל־הָ⁠עַמִּֽים

"all the peoples"

This could mean: (1) all the nations of the world. Alternate translation: [all the world’s nations] (2) the Israelite nation. Alternate translation: [all of the Israelites]

title: Zechariah 11:11 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תֻּפַ֖ר

"And it was broken"

The expression it was broken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I broke it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 11:11 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תֻּפַ֖ר

"And it was broken"

The pronoun it refers to the covenant that Yahweh had made with all the peoples, mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the covenant was broken]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 11:12 (#1)
content:
אִם־ט֧וֹב בְּ⁠עֵינֵי⁠כֶ֛ם הָב֥וּ שְׂכָרִ֖⁠י וְ⁠אִם־לֹ֣א ׀ חֲדָ֑לוּ

"If it is good in your eyes, give my wages; but if not, refrain"

Zechariah is presenting a possible condition, that the people may or may not think it is good to give him his wages. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If it is good in your eyes, then give my wages; but if it is not good, then refrain]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Zechariah 11:12 (#2)
content:
אִם־ט֧וֹב בְּ⁠עֵינֵי⁠כֶ֛ם

"If it is good in your eyes"

Zechariah is using good in your eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean that something seems good or right to a person. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If you consider it good]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 11:12 (#3)
content:
שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים כָּֽסֶף

"thirty {pieces} of silver"

In ancient times, a piece of silver was a coin or weight of silver called a shekel, which weighed about 11 grams, or about a third of an ounce. You could try to express this in terms of modern money values, but if you did, that could cause your Bible translation to become outdated and inaccurate, since those values can change over time. Instead, you might say something general like “thirty silver coins,” or give the equivalent weight, or use the term in the text and give the weight in a note.

See: Biblical Money

title: Zechariah 11:13 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠יּוֹצֵ֔ר & הַ⁠יּוֹצֵֽר

"the potter & the potter"

A potter is a kind of craftsman who forms objects out of clay. If your readers would not be familiar with what a potter is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the craftsman who makes things out of clay … the craftsman who makes things out of clay]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 11:13 (#2)
content:
אֶ֣דֶר הַ⁠יְקָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָקַ֖רְתִּי

"the magnificence of the price at which I was valued"

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here, since thirty pieces of silver was in fact a contemptibly small price. It was also the amount the owner of an ox that gored a slave to death had to give to the owner of the slave (see Exo 21:32), so by paying that amount they were saying he was worth the same as a dead slave.
