If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the contemptibly small price at which I was valued]

See: Irony

title: Zechariah 11:13 (#3)
content:
אֶ֣דֶר הַ⁠יְקָ֔ר

"the magnificence of the price"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of price, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the magnificent silver]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 11:14 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הָֽ⁠אַחֲוָ֔ה

"the brotherhood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of brotherhood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the brotherly ties]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 11:15 (#1)
content:
כְּלִ֖י רֹעֶ֥ה אֱוִלִֽי

"the equipment of a foolish shepherd"

Yahweh is speaking of a ruler of the people as if he were a shepherd. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the equipment of a foolish ruler]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:15 (#2)
content:
רֹעֶ֥ה אֱוִלִֽי

"a foolish shepherd"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific foolish shepherd. He means foolish shepherds in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [foolish shepherds]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 11:16 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י הִנֵּֽה

"for behold"

Here the word for introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [illustrating that]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 11:16 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠נִּכְחָד֤וֹת לֹֽא־יִפְקֹד֙ הַ⁠נַּ֣עַר לֹֽא־יְבַקֵּ֔שׁ וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּשְׁבֶּ֖רֶת לֹ֣א יְרַפֵּ֑א הַ⁠נִּצָּבָה֙ לֹ֣א יְכַלְכֵּ֔ל וּ⁠בְשַׂ֤ר הַ⁠בְּרִיאָה֙ יֹאכַ֔ל וּ⁠פַרְסֵי⁠הֶ֖ן יְפָרֵֽק

"He will not attend to the ones being destroyed; he will not seek the scattered one; and he will not heal the broken one; he will not sustain the one standing; but he will eat the flesh of the fat one, and he will tear off their hooves"

Zechariah uses a repetitive series of clauses here to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

See: Litany

title: Zechariah 11:16 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠בְּרִיאָה֙

"the fat one"

Here Zechariah is speaking as if the strongest, healthiest members of the people were the fat one, a well-fed sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the best-fed sheep] or [the strongest of the people]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 11:16 (#4)
content:
הִנֵּֽה

"behold"

Yahweh is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look, I am raising up a shepherd in the land]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 11:17 (#1)
content:
ה֣וֹי

"Woe"

Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of distress and warning of coming judgment. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas]

See: Exclamations

title: Zechariah 11:17 (#2)
content:
עַל־זְרוֹע֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַל־עֵ֣ין יְמִינ֑⁠וֹ

"against his arm and against his right eye"

Here, his arm represents the shepherd’s strength and his right eye represents his ability to see. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against his strong arm and against his seeing right eye]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 11:17 (#3)
content:
חֶ֥רֶב עַל־זְרוֹע֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַל־עֵ֣ין יְמִינ֑⁠וֹ

"A sword against his arm and against his right eye"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May a sword strike his arm and his right eye]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 11:17 (#4)
content:
חֶ֥רֶב

"A sword"

Here, A sword represents “a violent attack.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A violent attack]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 11:17 (#5)
content:
זְרֹע⁠וֹ֙ יָב֣וֹשׁ תִּיבָ֔שׁ וְ⁠עֵ֥ין יְמִינ֖⁠וֹ כָּהֹ֥ה תִכְהֶֽה

"His arm withering will wither, and his right eye dimming will dim"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [his arm will surely wither, and his right eye will surely grow dim]

See: Poetry

title: Zechariah - Chapter 12 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 12 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a new oracle in which Yahweh promises to defend Jerusalem and Judah against the nations that attack them (verses 1–9), then to pour out grief so that the people mourn over “the one whom they pierced” (verses 10–14). The repeated phrase “on that day” marks these as future events.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The one whom they pierced

In verse 10 the pronouns shift from “me” to “him” for the pierced one. Preserve this ambiguity rather than deciding to whom these pronouns refer.

title: Zechariah 12:1 (#1)
content:
מַשָּׂ֥א דְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"The burden of the word of Yahweh concerning Israel"

Zechariah is using the words translated as The burden of the word of Yahweh concerning Israel to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 12:1 (#2)
content:
מַשָּׂ֥א דְבַר־יְהוָ֖ה

"The burden of the word of Yahweh"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the message from Yahweh as if it were a burden, that is, a heavy load that a person must carry. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The severe word of Yahweh]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:1 (#3)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֗ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Zechariah is using the declaration of Yahweh to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 12:1 (#4)
content:
נֹטֶ֤ה שָׁמַ֨יִם֙ וְ⁠יֹסֵ֣ד אָ֔רֶץ

"the one stretching out the heavens and founding the earth"

Here Zechariah is speaking of how Yahweh made the world as if he were stretching out a tent to form the heavens and founding a building to form the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who made the heavens and who made the earth]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:1 (#5)
content:
רֽוּחַ־אָדָ֖ם

"the spirit of man"

This phrase continues the references to creation. The spirit of man represents “life.” The word translated man could also be transliterated as “Adam.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the life of a person] or [Adam’s life]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 12:2 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֣ה אָ֠נֹכִי שָׂ֣ם

"Behold, I am making"

This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 12:2 (#2)
content:
הִנֵּ֣ה

"Behold"

Zechariah is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 12:2 (#3)
content:
סַף־רַ֛עַל לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עַמִּ֖ים סָבִ֑יב

"a cup of staggering for all of the peoples all around"

Here Yahweh is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were a cup of staggering, that is, a cup of wine that would make the surrounding nations drunk so that they reel and cannot stand. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a source of helpless reeling for all of the peoples all around]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:2 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠גַ֧ם עַל־יְהוּדָ֛ה יִֽהְיֶ֥ה בַ⁠מָּצ֖וֹר עַל־יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

"And also against Judah it will be, in the siege against Jerusalem"

This could mean: (1) Judah and Jerusalem are besieged. Alternate translation: [And just as Jerusalem is besieged, so is all of Judah.] (2) Judah is going to besiege Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [Judah joins the nations to besiege Jerusalem.]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 12:3 (#1)
content:
אֶ֤בֶן מַֽעֲמָסָה֙ לְ⁠כָל־הָ֣⁠עַמִּ֔ים

"a stone of burden for all of the peoples"

Here Yahweh is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were a stone of burden, that is, a stone so heavy that anyone who tries to lift it injures himself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a burden too heavy for all of the peoples]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:3 (#2)
content:
שָׂר֣וֹט יִשָּׂרֵ֑טוּ

"injuring, will be injured"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb injuring in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [will certainly be severely injured]

See: Reduplication

title: Zechariah 12:3 (#3)
content:
כָּל־עֹמְסֶ֖י⁠הָ

"All of the ones lifting it"

Yahweh is using the participle the ones lifting it as a noun to mean a certain kind of person, namely, the nations who try to take Jerusalem for themselves. Your language may use participles in the same way. If not, you can translate this participle with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [All of the nations who try to lift it]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 12:3 (#4)
content:
שָׂר֣וֹט יִשָּׂרֵ֑טוּ

"injuring, will be injured"

The expression will be injured is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will surely injure themselves severely]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 12:3 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נֶאֶסְפ֣וּ עָלֶ֔י⁠הָ כֹּ֖ל גּוֹיֵ֥י הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"and all of the nations of the earth will be gathered against it"

The expression will be gathered is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of the nations of the earth will assemble themselves against it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 12:4 (#1)
content:
אַכֶּ֤ה כָל־סוּס֙ בַּ⁠תִּמָּה֔וֹן וְ⁠רֹכְב֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠שִּׁגָּע֑וֹן

"I will strike every horse with confusion and its rider with madness"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of confusion and madness, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [I will strike every horse so that it becomes bewildered and its rider so that he becomes crazed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 12:4 (#2)
content:
בֵּ֤ית יְהוּדָה֙

"the house of Judah"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were a house, a single household. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Judean people]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:4 (#3)
content:
אֶפְקַ֣ח אֶת־עֵינַ֔⁠י

"I will open my eyes"

Yahweh is using I will open my eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will watch over and protect.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will keep watch protectively]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 12:4 (#4)
content:
כָל־סוּס֙ בַּ⁠תִּמָּה֔וֹן וְ⁠רֹכְב֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠שִּׁגָּע֑וֹן & וְ⁠כֹל֙ ס֣וּס הָֽ⁠עַמִּ֔ים

"every horse with confusion and its rider with madness & and every horse of the peoples"

Yahweh is using every horse, every horse of the peoples, and its rider to represent the whole army of the enemy nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the enemy forces with confusion and their soldiers with madness … every horse of the enemy]

See: Synecdoche

title: Zechariah 12:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָֽמְר֛וּ אַלֻּפֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה בְּ⁠לִבָּ֑⁠ם

"And the chiefs of Judah will say in their heart"

Zechariah is using will say in their heart as a common expression of the culture to mean “will say to themselves” or “will think.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the chiefs of Judah will think to themselves]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 12:5 (#2)
content:
אַמְצָ֥ה לִ⁠י֙ יֹשְׁבֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם בַּ⁠יהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת אֱלֹהֵי⁠הֶֽם

"The inhabitants of Jerusalem are a strength to me by Yahweh of Armies, their God"

The words that the chiefs of Judah say are a quotation within Yahweh’s quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that the dwellers of Jerusalem are strength for them through Yahweh of Armies, their God]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 12:5 (#3)
content:
אַמְצָ֥ה לִ⁠י֙ יֹשְׁבֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם

"The inhabitants of Jerusalem are a strength to me"

This could mean: (1) the people who live in Jerusalem are strong because Yahweh of Armies their God is with them or (2) the people who live in Jerusalem are a source of strength for the chiefs of Judah. You could make this information explicit if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The dwellers of Jerusalem are a source of strength to me]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 12:5 (#4)
content:
אַמְצָ֥ה לִ⁠י֙

"are a strength to me"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of strength, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [strengthen me]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 12:5 (#5)
content:
לִ⁠י֙

"to me"

The pronoun me is singular, referring to each chief of Judah individually, even though all the chiefs are speaking. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to each of us]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#1)
content:
כְּֽ⁠כִיּ֧וֹר אֵ֣שׁ בְּ⁠עֵצִ֗ים וּ⁠כְ⁠לַפִּ֥יד אֵשׁ֙ בְּ⁠עָמִ֔יר

"like a basin of fire among trees and like a torch of fire in a sheaf"

The point of this comparison is that just as a basin of fire among trees and a torch of fire in a sheaf quickly burn up everything around them, so the chiefs of Judah will destroy the peoples around them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [able to consume their enemies as quickly as a firepot burns up wood and as a flaming torch burns up a sheaf of grain]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#2)
content:
כְּֽ⁠כִיּ֧וֹר אֵ֣שׁ

"like a basin of fire"

A basin is a kind of large, open container that can hold burning coals or fire. If your readers would not be familiar with what a basin of this kind is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a pot full of burning coals]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠עָמִ֔יר

"in a sheaf"

A sheaf is a bundle of cut grain stalks tied together. When dried, it is highly flammable. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sheaf is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [bundle of cut grain]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אָ֨כְל֜וּ

"and they will devour"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the chiefs of Judah destroying their enemies as if they would devour them the way fire consumes what it burns. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will destroy]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#5)
content:
עַל־יָמִ֧ין וְ⁠עַל־שְׂמֹ֛אול

"on the right and on the left"

Yahweh is referring to every direction by naming two major components, the right and the left. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in every direction]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יָשְׁבָ֨ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֥ם ע֛וֹד תַּחְתֶּ֖י⁠הָ

"And Jerusalem will dwell again in its place"

Here, Jerusalem represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the people of Jerusalem will dwell again in their place]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 12:6 (#7)
content:
תַּחְתֶּ֖י⁠הָ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם

"in its place, in Jerusalem"

It might seem that the expression in its place, in Jerusalem contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [in its own place]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Zechariah 12:7 (#1)
content:
לְמַ֨עַן

"so that"

Here, so that marks the honor of the house of David and the honor of the dweller of Jerusalem will not be great over Judah as the goal or purpose of Yahweh saving the tents of Judah first. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that]

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Zechariah 12:7 (#2)
content:
אֶת־אָהֳלֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה

"the tents of Judah"

Here, the tents of Judah represents the homes and households of the people of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the households of Judah]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 12:7 (#3)
content:
תִּפְאֶ֣רֶת בֵּית־דָּוִ֗יד וְ⁠תִפְאֶ֛רֶת יֹשֵׁ֥ב יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם

"the honor of the house of David and the honor of the dweller of Jerusalem"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of honor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the honored house of David and the honored dweller of Jerusalem]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 12:7 (#4)
content:
בֵּית־דָּוִ֗יד

"the house of David"

Here Zechariah is speaking of the descendants of King David, the royal family, as if they were a house, a single household. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the royal family descended from David]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:7 (#5)
content:
יֹשֵׁ֥ב יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם

"the dweller of Jerusalem"

Zechariah is not referring to a specific dweller of Jerusalem. He means the people who live in Jerusalem in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the residents of Jerusalem]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 12:7 (#6)
content:
לֹֽא־תִגְדַּ֜ל תִּפְאֶ֣רֶת בֵּית־דָּוִ֗יד וְ⁠תִפְאֶ֛רֶת יֹשֵׁ֥ב יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם עַל־יְהוּדָֽה

"the honor of the house of David and the honor of the dweller of Jerusalem will not be great over Judah"

Zechariah is using will not be great over Judah as a common expression of the culture to mean “will not be considered more important than the rest of Judah.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the honor of the house of David and the honor of the dweller of Jerusalem will not be regarded as more important than the honor of the rest of Judah]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 12:8 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠נִּכְשָׁ֥ל בָּ⁠הֶ֛ם

"and the stumbler among them"

Here Zechariah is speaking of a weak or feeble person as if he were a stumbler. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the weakest one among them]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:8 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠נִּכְשָׁ֥ל

"and the stumbler"

Zechariah is using the adjective stumbler as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the one who stumbles]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 12:8 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֞ה & כְּ⁠דָוִ֑יד וּ⁠בֵ֤ית דָּוִיד֙ כֵּֽ⁠אלֹהִ֔ים

"will be like David, and the house of David, like God"

Zechariah says will be like David, and the house of David, like God as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [will be strong like David was, and the house of David will seem as powerful as God]

See: Hyperbole

title: Zechariah 12:8 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בֵ֤ית דָּוִיד֙ כֵּֽ⁠אלֹהִ֔ים

"and the house of David, like God"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. It may be helpful to repeat them from the earlier phrase. Alternate translation: [and the house of David will be like God]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 12:8 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בֵ֤ית דָּוִיד֙ כֵּֽ⁠אלֹהִ֔ים כְּ⁠מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה

"and the house of David, like God, like the angel of Yahweh"

The point of this comparison is that just as God and the angel of Yahweh are powerful, so the house of David will be powerful as they lead the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the house of David will be as powerful as God is, as powerful as the angel of Yahweh]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 12:8 (#6)
content:
כְּ⁠מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶֽם

"like the angel of Yahweh to their face"

Here, their face represents their presence, so the phrase means going ahead of the people to lead them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [like having the angel of Yahweh fighting in front of them]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 12:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֖ה בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֑וּא אֲבַקֵּ֗שׁ לְ⁠הַשְׁמִיד֙ אֶת־כָּל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם הַ⁠בָּאִ֖ים עַל־יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

"And it will be on that day, I will seek to destroy all of the nations coming against Jerusalem"

Here Yahweh’s direct speech resumes after the narration of the previous verses. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 12:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁפַכְתִּי֩

"And I will pour out"

Here Yahweh is speaking of generously giving his spirit to people as if he would pour out a liquid on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will generously bestow]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 12:10 (#2)
content:
ר֤וּחַ חֵן֙ וְ⁠תַ֣חֲנוּנִ֔ים

"a spirit of favor and supplications"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of favor and supplications, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [a spirit that causes me to be pleased with them to plead with me and causes me to be pleased with them]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 12:10 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִבִּ֥יטוּ אֵלַ֖⁠י אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־דָּקָ֑רוּ וְ⁠סָפְד֣וּ עָלָ֗י⁠ו

"and they will look to me, whom they pierced. And they will mourn over him"

The pronoun him refers to the same person as me earlier in the verse. Yahweh shifts here from speaking of himself in the first person to speaking of the pierced one in the third person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and they will look to me, whom they pierced. And they will mourn over the one they pierced]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 12:10 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠סָפְד֣וּ עָלָ֗י⁠ו כְּ⁠מִסְפֵּד֙ עַל־הַ⁠יָּחִ֔יד

"And they will mourn over him as the mourning over the only one"

The point of this comparison is that just as people grieve very deeply for the only one, that is, an only child who has died, so the people will mourn over the one whom they pierced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And they will mourn over him as deeply as people grieve for an only child who has died]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 12:10 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הָמֵ֥ר עָלָ֖י⁠ו כְּ⁠הָמֵ֥ר עַֽל־הַ⁠בְּכֽוֹר

"and they will be bitter over him as being bitter over the firstborn"

The point of this comparison is that just as people grieve bitterly over the firstborn, that is, a firstborn son who has died, so the people will grieve bitterly over the one whom they pierced. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they will weep powerfully over him, just as people weep powerfully when a firstborn son dies]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 12:11 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠מִסְפַּ֥ד הֲדַדְ־רִמּ֖וֹן בְּ⁠בִקְעַ֥ת מְגִדּֽוֹן

"like the mourning of Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo"

The point of this comparison is that just as the mourning of Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo was a well-known time of very great grief, so the mourning in Jerusalem will be very great. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as great as the well-known grief at Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 12:11 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠מִסְפַּ֥ד הֲדַדְ־רִמּ֖וֹן

"like the mourning of Hadad Rimmon"

This could mean: (1) the weeping for King Josiah, who was killed at Megiddo and for whom the people mourned greatly, Alternate translation: [like the mourning for King Josiah at Hadad Rimmon] or (2) the ritual mourning for a god named Hadad Rimmon, or (3) both. You could include this information in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 12:11 (#3)
content:
הֲדַדְ־רִמּ֖וֹן בְּ⁠בִקְעַ֥ת מְגִדּֽוֹן

"Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megiddo"

The word Hadad Rimmon is the name of a place, and the word Megiddo is the name of a place.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 12:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠סָפְדָ֣ה הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ

"And the land will mourn"

Here, the land represents the people who live in the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And everyone living in the land will mourn]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 12:12 (#2)
content:
מִשְׁפָּח֥וֹת מִשְׁפָּח֖וֹת לְ⁠בָ֑ד

"clans, clans separately"

Zechariah is repeating the term clans in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys, that each clan mourns by itself. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [each and every clan will mourn separately]

See: Reduplication

title: Zechariah 12:12 (#3)
content:
מִשְׁפַּ֨חַת בֵּית־דָּוִ֤יד לְ⁠בָד֙ וּ⁠נְשֵׁי⁠הֶ֣ם לְ⁠בָ֔ד מִשְׁפַּ֤חַת בֵּית־נָתָן֙ לְ⁠בָ֔ד וּ⁠נְשֵׁי⁠הֶ֖ם לְ⁠בָֽד

"the clan of the house of David separately, and their wives separately; the clan of the house of Nathan separately, and their wives separately"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The men of the clan of the house of David will mourn by themselves and the women of that clan will mourn by themselves. The men of the clan descended from Nathan will mourn by themselves and the women of that clan will mourn by themselves]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 12:12 (#4)
content:
בֵּית־נָתָן֙

"the house of Nathan"

This could mean: (1) Nathan, the son of King David, Alternate translation: [the house of Nathan, David’s son] or (2) Nathan, the prophet who served during David’s reign. Alternate translation: [the house of prophet Nathan] You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 12:12–14 (#1)
content:
מִשְׁפַּ֨חַת בֵּית־דָּוִ֤יד לְ⁠בָד֙ וּ⁠נְשֵׁי⁠הֶ֣ם לְ⁠בָ֔ד

"the clan of the house of David separately, and their wives separately"

In some languages, the repeated systematic repetition of the rest of verse 12 through verse 14 may not give a similar emphasis to the deepness and powerfulness of the mourning that will happen. Translate in a way that emphasizes how strong the grief was in a natural way in your language. Alternate translation: [the clans of David, Nathan, Levi, and the Shimeite will all mourn very intensely; the men and women will mourn separately, in their own ways]

See: Information Structure

title: Zechariah 12:12–14 (#2)
content:
מִשְׁפַּ֨חַת בֵּית־דָּוִ֤יד לְ⁠בָד֙ וּ⁠נְשֵׁי⁠הֶ֣ם לְ⁠בָ֔ד

"the clan of the house of David separately, and their wives separately"

Zechariah assumes that readers will know that the separation of men and women in public mourning reflects the mourning customs of that society. Translate this so readers do not misinterpret it as marital strife or divorce. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [According to custom, each clan will mourn by itself, and men and women will mourn separately]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 12:13 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠שִּׁמְעִי֙

"the Shimeite"

The word Shimeite is the name of a people group, the descendants of a man named Shimei.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 12:14 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֗ל הַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּחוֹת֙ הַ⁠נִּשְׁאָר֔וֹת

"all of the clans, the ones remaining"

Zechariah is using the adjective the ones remaining as a noun to mean certain clans, namely, all the other clans that have not yet been named. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and any other clans]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah - Chapter 13 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 13 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Verses 1–6 are a prose oracle about cleansing from sin and removing false prophets. Verses 7–9 shift to poetry, announcing the striking of Yahweh’s shepherd and the purifying of a surviving remnant.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The Prophetic Cloak

The “cloak of hair” (verse 4) is the rough garment that identified prophets. False prophets abandon this clothing to conceal their identity.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Nested Quotations

Yahweh’s speech spans the entire chapter and contains embedded quotes from parents (verse 3), a false prophet (verses 5–6), and a covenant declaration (verse 9).

title: Zechariah 13:1 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֗וּא

"On that day"

Zechariah is using the phrase On that day to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. See the Introduction to Zechariah for a discussion of the similar phrase “in that day.”

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 13:1 (#2)
content:
מָק֣וֹר נִפְתָּ֔ח

"a fountain & opened"

Here Zechariah is speaking as if the means of cleansing from sin were a fountain that would be opened. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a source of cleansing will be made available]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:1 (#3)
content:
יִֽהְיֶה֙ מָק֣וֹר נִפְתָּ֔ח

"a fountain will be opened"

The expression a fountain will be opened is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will open a fountain]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 13:1 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֥ית דָּוִ֖יד

"for the house of David"

Here, the house of David represents the descendants of David and the royal dynasty. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people descended from David]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 13:1 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠חַטַּ֖את וּ⁠לְ⁠נִדָּֽה

"for sin and for impurity"

Zechariah is referring to all types of uncleanness by naming two major components, sin and impurity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every kind of sin and ritual uncleanness]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 13:1 (#6)
content:
לְ⁠חַטַּ֖את וּ⁠לְ⁠נִדָּֽה

"for sin and for impurity"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of sin and impurity, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [cleansing you from your sinning and from your being unclean]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 13:2 (#1)
content:
אֶת־שְׁמ֤וֹת הָֽ⁠עֲצַבִּים֙

"the names of the idols"

Here, the names of the idols represents the memory and reputation of the idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the memory of the idols]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 13:2 (#2)
content:
נְאֻ֣ם ׀ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

The phrase the declaration of Yahweh of Armies is a parenthetical statement within Yahweh’s speech that identifies him as the speaker. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the speaker of a direct quotation in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 13:2 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִזָּכְר֖וּ ע֑וֹד

"and they will not be remembered again"

The expression they will not be remembered again is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one will remember them anymore]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 13:2 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠טֻּמְאָ֖ה

"uncleanness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of uncleanness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is unclean]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 13:2 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠גַ֧ם

"and also"

Here, the words and also add a further action to the one just described. Yahweh will not only remove the idols but will additionally remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and furthermore,]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Zechariah 13:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֗ה כִּֽי־יִנָּבֵ֣א אִישׁ֮ עוֹד֒

"And it will happen, when a man prophesies again"

Zechariah is presenting a possible condition, that a man will prophesy falsely again and, as a result, his own father and mother will condemn and kill him. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [If a man prophesies falsely again]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Zechariah 13:3 (#2)
content:
אִישׁ֮

"a man"

Zechariah is not referring to a specific man. He means men in general who prophesy. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any man] or [anyone]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 13:3 (#3)
content:
יֹֽלְדָי⁠ו֙

"the ones bearing him"

Zechariah is not distinguishing this father and mother from another father and mother who are not the ones bearing him. He is reminding readers that the man’s own parents are the ones who gave birth to him. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [who themselves gave him birth]

See: Distinguishing Versus Informing or Reminding

title: Zechariah 13:3 (#4)
content:
לֹ֣א תִֽחְיֶ֔ה כִּ֛י שֶׁ֥קֶר דִּבַּ֖רְתָּ בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה

"You will not live, for you have spoken falsehood in the name of Yahweh"

The father and mother’s words are a quotation within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that he will not live, for he has spoken falsehood in the name of Yahweh]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 13:3 (#5)
content:
שֶׁ֥קֶר דִּבַּ֖רְתָּ

"you have spoken falsehood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of falsehood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you have spoken falsely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 13:3 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה

"in the name of Yahweh"

Here, the name of Yahweh represents the authority of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as one who has Yahweh’s authority]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 13:4 (#1)
content:
יֵבֹ֧שׁוּ הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֛ים

"the prophets will have shame"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of shame, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the prophets will be ashamed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 13:4 (#2)
content:
אַדֶּ֥רֶת שֵׂעָ֖ר

"a cloak of hair"

The implication is that a cloak of hair was the distinctive garment that prophets wore, so putting it on was a way of claiming to be a prophet. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the hairy cloak that marks a person as a prophet]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 13:5 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠נְּעוּרָֽ⁠י

"from my youth"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of youth, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [since I was a boy]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 13:5 (#2)
content:
אֲדָמָה֙ & כִּ֥י אָדָ֖ם הִקְנַ֥⁠נִי מִ⁠נְּעוּרָֽ⁠י

"the ground, for a man has owned me from my youth"

This could mean: (1) that the person is tied to this land and working this land because he is a bondservant or slave to the owner. Alternate translation: [this ground that my master from my youth owns] (2) that he owns this land (requires reading the Hebrew slightly differently). That is, he’s a small landowner or a subsistence farmer and is tied to the land. Alternate translation: [the little patch of ground I have owned since I was young]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Zechariah 13:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַ֣ר אֵלָ֔י⁠ו מָ֧ה הַ⁠מַּכּ֛וֹת הָ⁠אֵ֖לֶּה בֵּ֣ין יָדֶ֑י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אָמַ֕ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֻכֵּ֖יתִי בֵּ֥ית מְאַהֲבָֽ⁠י

"And {someone} will say to him, ‘What are these wounds between your hands?’ And he will say, ‘Those are the ones with which I was struck {in} the house of my lovers"

The question and its answer here are quotations within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And someone will ask him what those wounds between his hands are. And he will say that those are the ones with which he was struck in the house of his lovers]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah 13:6 (#2)
content:
בֵּ֣ין יָדֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"between your hands"

The speaker is using between your hands as a common expression of the culture to mean “on the front of the body.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the front of your body]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 13:6 (#3)
content:
הֻכֵּ֖יתִי

"I was struck"

The expression I was struck is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people struck me]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 13:6 (#4)
content:
בֵּ֥ית מְאַהֲבָֽ⁠י

"in} the house of my lovers"

This could mean: (1) that the speaker is saying he was injured somehow while at the home of friends, perhaps in a drunken brawl or something. Alternate translation: [when I got in a fight with some local people] (2) that the speaker is speaking of the false gods that he worshiped as if they were his lovers. Idol worship sometimes involves self-mutilation. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the temples of the false gods I worshiped]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#1)
content:
חֶ֗רֶב עוּרִ֤י עַל־רֹעִ⁠י֙

"Sword, awake against my shepherd"

Yahweh is speaking to a Sword that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that is coming on his shepherd. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the sword. Alternate translation: [May the sword awake against my shepherd]

See: Apostrophe

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#2)
content:
חֶ֗רֶב עוּרִ֤י עַל־רֹעִ⁠י֙

"Sword, awake against my shepherd"

Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man, my companion—Yahweh is using the term Sword to represent the violent death that a sword can inflict. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Someone, kill my shepherd with a sword]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#3)
content:
נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh of Armies"

Zechariah is using the declaration of Yahweh of Armies to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#4)
content:
רֹעִ⁠י֙ & אֶת־הָֽ⁠רֹעֶה֙

"my shepherd & the shepherd"

Yahweh is speaking of the leader of his people as if he were a shepherd. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leader of my people … the leader of my people]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠תְפוּצֶ֣יןָ הַ⁠צֹּ֔אן

"and the flock will scatter"

Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my people will scatter]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠הֲשִׁבֹתִ֥י יָדִ֖⁠י עַל

"and I will turn my hand against"

Here, hand represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will use my power against]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 13:7 (#7)
content:
הַ⁠צֹּעֲרִֽים

"the little ones"

Yahweh is using the adjective little ones as a noun to mean a certain kind of person, those who are lowly and insignificant. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the ones who are insignificant]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 13:8 (#1)
content:
פִּֽי־שְׁנַ֣יִם בָּ֔⁠הּ יִכָּרְת֖וּ יִגְוָ֑עוּ וְ⁠הַ⁠שְּׁלִשִׁ֖ית יִוָּ֥תֶר בָּֽ⁠הּ

"two portions in it will be cut off, they will expire, and the third will be left in it"

The expression two portions means two parts out of three equal parts, that is, two-thirds of the people. And the third means one part out of three equal parts, that is, one-third of the people.

See: Fractions

title: Zechariah 13:8 (#2)
content:
פִּֽי־שְׁנַ֣יִם בָּ֔⁠הּ יִכָּרְת֖וּ

"two portions in it will be cut off"

The expression will be cut off is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will cut off two portions in it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 13:8 (#3)
content:
יִכָּרְת֖וּ

"will be cut off"

Yahweh is speaking of people being killed as if they were parts of something that could be cut off, such as cutting branches from a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be killed]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:8 (#4)
content:
יִגְוָ֑עוּ

"they will expire"

Yahweh is speaking of the people who will die as if their lives were a breath that will expire, or run out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [breathe their last breath] or [die]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:8 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠שְּׁלִשִׁ֖ית יִוָּ֥תֶר בָּֽ⁠הּ

"and the third will be left in it"

The expression will be left is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will leave the third in it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵבֵאתִ֤י אֶת־הַ⁠שְּׁלִשִׁית֙ בָּ⁠אֵ֔שׁ

"And I will bring the third into the fire"

Yahweh is speaking of the suffering he will use to purify his people as if it were a fire. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will bring the third through purifying suffering]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠צְרַפְתִּי⁠ם֙ כִּ⁠צְרֹ֣ף אֶת־הַ⁠כֶּ֔סֶף וּ⁠בְחַנְתִּ֖י⁠ם כִּ⁠בְחֹ֣ן אֶת־הַ⁠זָּהָ֑ב

"and I will refine them as {one} refines the silver, and I will test them as {one} tests the gold"

The point of this comparison is that just as one refines the silver and tests the gold to remove impurities and prove them genuine, so Yahweh will purify his people through suffering and prove that they are genuine. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I will purify them the way that one refines silver to remove its impurities, and I will prove them genuine the way that one tests gold]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#3)
content:
ה֣וּא

"He"

The pronoun He refers to the surviving third of the people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The surviving third, they]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#4)
content:
ה֣וּא ׀ יִקְרָ֣א בִ⁠שְׁמִ֗⁠י וַֽ⁠אֲנִי֙ אֶעֱנֶ֣ה

"He, he will call on my name, and I, I will answer"

Yahweh is stating the pronouns He and I along with the verbs translated as he will call and I will answer, which already include their meanings. He is doing that because he is contrasting what the remnant of his people will do with what he himself will do. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for them, they will call on my name, and as for me, I will answer him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#5)
content:
יִקְרָ֣א בִ⁠שְׁמִ֗⁠י

"he will call on my name"

Yahweh is using call on my name as a common expression of the culture to mean “to worship me and pray to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will worship me and pray to me]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#6)
content:
עַמִּ֣⁠י ה֔וּא & יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י

"He is my people & Yahweh is my God"

The implication is that He is my people and Yahweh is my God are the words of a covenant, expressing the restored relationship in which Yahweh claims these people as his own and they acknowledge him as their God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He is the people I claim as my own … Yahweh is the one I acknowledge as my God]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 13:9 (#7)
content:
עַמִּ֣⁠י ה֔וּא וְ⁠ה֥וּא יֹאמַ֖ר יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י

"He is my people,’ and he, he will say, ‘Yahweh is my God"

There are quotations within a quotation here. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that he is my people, and he, he will say that Yahweh is his God]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Zechariah - Chapter 14 Introduction
content:
Zechariah 14 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This closing chapter is a prose oracle about the day of Yahweh: the nations attack Jerusalem (verses 1–8), Yahweh reigns as king (verses 9–11), he strikes the attackers (verses 12–15), and the survivors come to worship him (verses 16–21).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The climax of the book

Zechariah 14:20–21 presents a picture of universal holiness, where ordinary domestic objects carry the same sacredness as the High Priest’s crown. In Exodus 28:36, this inscription belonged exclusively to the High Priest’s golden crown. Here it is stamped on common horse bells and kitchen pots, signifying that in the messianic kingdom, the boundary between the sacred and the everyday is abolished, and all of life and creation becomes completely holy to God. Compare this to Isaiah 11:9 and Habakkuk 2:14, where the holy presence and knowledge of God fill the entire earth.

The day of Yahweh

The repeated phrase “on that day” marks the time when Yahweh judges the nations and establishes his rule. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/dayofthelord]].

The Festival of Booths

This was a yearly Israelite festival during which people lived in temporary shelters. Here even the nations celebrate it.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Shifts in person

Yahweh speaks of himself as “I” in verse 2 but is spoken of as “he” elsewhere, so translators may need to make the speaker explicit.

title: Zechariah 14:1 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֥ה

"Behold"

Zechariah is using the term Behold to focus the attention of his listeners on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully]

See: Foreground Information

title: Zechariah 14:1 (#2)
content:
יֽוֹם־בָּ֖א לַֽ⁠יהוָ֑ה

"a day is coming for Yahweh"

Zechariah is using a day is coming for Yahweh as a common expression of the culture to mean “the time is coming when Yahweh will act to judge his enemies and rescue his people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time of Yahweh’s judgment is near]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:1 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠חֻלַּ֥ק שְׁלָלֵ֖⁠ךְ בְּ⁠קִרְבֵּֽ⁠ךְ

"and your spoil will be divided in your midst"

Zechariah is speaking to the city of Jerusalem, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about what will happen to the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [and the spoil taken from Jerusalem will be divided within that city]

See: Apostrophe

title: Zechariah 14:1 (#4)
content:
שְׁלָלֵ֖⁠ךְ בְּ⁠קִרְבֵּֽ⁠ךְ

"your spoil & in your midst"

The pronoun your refers to Jerusalem which (see verse 2) represents the people in Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 14:1 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠חֻלַּ֥ק שְׁלָלֵ֖⁠ךְ בְּ⁠קִרְבֵּֽ⁠ךְ

"and your spoil will be divided in your midst"

The expression will be divided is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and your enemies will divide your spoil in your midst]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 14:1 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠קִרְבֵּֽ⁠ךְ

"in your midst"

The word your is singular here because Zechariah is addressing the city of Jerusalem, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָסַפְתִּ֨י אֶת־כָּל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֥ם ׀ אֶֽל־יְרוּשָׁלִַם֮

"And I will gather all the nations to Jerusalem"

Yahweh is speaking here. If it would be helpful in your language, you could that make clear. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh says, “I will gather all the nations to Jerusalem]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נִלְכְּדָ֣ה הָ⁠עִ֗יר וְ⁠נָשַׁ֨סּוּ֙ הַ⁠בָּ֣תִּ֔ים וְ⁠הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֖ים תשגלנה

"and the city will be captured, and the houses will be plundered, and the women will be raped"

The expressions will be captured, will be plundered, and will be raped are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the nations will capture the city, and they will plunder the houses, and they will rape the women]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֖ים תשגלנה

"and the women will be raped"

The oral reading tradition of the original language substitutes a less explicit word here, referring in a polite way to what the soldiers will do to the women. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and the women will be violated]

See: Euphemism

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יָצָ֞א חֲצִ֤י הָ⁠עִיר֙ בַּ⁠גּוֹלָ֔ה

"And half of the city will go out into the exile"

Here, the city represents “the people who live in the city.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And half of the city’s inhabitants will go out into the exile]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#5)
content:
חֲצִ֤י הָ⁠עִיר֙

"half of the city"

The fraction half means one part out of two equal parts of the people of the city. Alternate translation: [one of every two people]

See: Fractions

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#6)
content:
בַּ⁠גּוֹלָ֔ה

"into the exile"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of exile, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be forced to live in a foreign land]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠יֶ֣תֶר הָ⁠עָ֔ם לֹ֥א יִכָּרֵ֖ת מִן־הָ⁠עִֽיר

"but the rest of the people will not be cut off from the city"

Zechariah is speaking as if the rest of the people would literally ** not be cut off** from the city. He means that the enemies will not remove them from it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but the rest of the people will remain in the city]

See: Metaphor

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠יֶ֣תֶר הָ⁠עָ֔ם לֹ֥א יִכָּרֵ֖ת מִן־הָ⁠עִֽיר

"but the rest of the people will not be cut off from the city"

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle not and the negative word cut off. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [the rest of the people will remain in the city]

See: Double Negatives

title: Zechariah 14:2 (#9)
content:
וְ⁠יֶ֣תֶר הָ⁠עָ֔ם

"but the rest of the people"

Habakkuk uses the word but here to indicate a contrast between the half of the city that will go into exile and the rest of the people who will remain. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, the rest of the people]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 14:3 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠י֥וֹם הִֽלָּחֲמ֖⁠ו בְּ⁠י֥וֹם קְרָֽב

"like the day of his fighting on a day of battle"

The point of this comparison is that just as Yahweh fought powerfully for his people on a day of battle in the past, so he will fight against these nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as he fought powerfully for his people in past battles]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 14:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָמְד֣וּ רַגְלָ֣י⁠ו

"And his feet will stand"

Zechariah is using his feet, one part of Yahweh, to represent all of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will stand]

See: Synecdoche

title: Zechariah 14:4 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּוֹם־הַ֠⁠הוּא

"on that day"

Zechariah is using on that day as a common expression of the culture to mean “at the time when Yahweh will act to judge the nations and rescue his people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on that day of judgment and deliverance]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:4 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֨ר עַל־פְּנֵ֥י יְרוּשָׁלִַם֮ מִ⁠קֶּדֶם֒

"which is on the face of Jerusalem from the east"

Here, the face of Jerusalem represents “the area in front of Jerusalem.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which is in front of Jerusalem on the east]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 14:4 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠נִבְקַע֩ הַ֨ר הַ⁠זֵּיתִ֤ים מֵֽ⁠חֶצְי⁠וֹ֙ מִזְרָ֣חָ⁠ה וָ⁠יָ֔מָּ⁠ה

"And the Mount of Olives will be split from its half toward the east and toward the west"

The expression will be split is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Mount of Olives will split apart down the middle, from east to west, forming]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 14:4 (#5)
content:
גֵּ֖יא גְּדוֹלָ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד

"a very great valley"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [creating a very great valley]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 14:4 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠חֶצְי⁠וֹ־נֶֽגְבָּ⁠ה

"and its half toward the south"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and its other half will move away toward the south]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 14:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נַסְתֶּ֣ם גֵּֽיא־הָרַ֗⁠י כִּֽי־יַגִּ֣יעַ גֵּי־הָרִים֮ אֶל־אָצַל֒

"And you will flee {by} the valley of my mountains, for the valley of the mountains will reach to Azal"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because the valley of the mountains will reach to Azal, you will flee by the valley of my mountains]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Zechariah 14:5 (#2)
content:
אָצַל֒

"Azal"

The word Azal is the name of a place.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 14:5 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠רַ֔עַשׁ

"from the face of the earthquake"

Zechariah is using from the face of as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the earthquake that terrified you]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:5 (#4)
content:
בִּ⁠ימֵ֖י עֻזִּיָּ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה

"in the days of Uzziah the king of Judah"

The implication is that this was a well-known earthquake that the people of Judah still remembered. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the days of Uzziah the king of Judah, that earthquake everyone remembers]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 14:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֖ה בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֑וּא

"And it will happen on that day"

Zechariah is not using the phrase translated as And it will happen on that day to introduce a new event. In this and in the several following verses, he is using on that day to refer back to the appointed day introduced in verse 1. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for looking back to the same day. Alternate translation: [And it will happen on that same day]

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Zechariah 14:6 (#2)
content:
יְקָר֖וֹת

"the splendid"

Zechariah is using the adjective splendid as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the splendid heavenly bodies]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Zechariah 14:6 (#3)
content:
לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֣ה א֔וֹר יְקָר֖וֹת יקפאו⁠ן

"there will not be light; the splendid will congeal"

The implication is that the normal sources of light will fail on that day. This could mean: (1) that there will be no light and that instead there will be cold and frost, Alternate translation: [there will not be light; instead there will be cold and frost] or (2) that the bright heavenly bodies will no longer shine. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the sun, moon, and stars will stop shining]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 14:7 (#1)
content:
ה֛וּא יִוָּדַ֥ע לַֽ⁠יהוָ֖ה

"it, it will be known to Yahweh"

The expression will be known is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will know about it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 14:7 (#2)
content:
לֹא־י֣וֹם וְ⁠לֹא־לָ֑יְלָה

"not day and not night"

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [it will not be day and it will not be night]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 14:7 (#3)
content:
לֹא־י֣וֹם וְ⁠לֹא־לָ֑יְלָה

"not day and not night"

Zechariah is using the two parts of a full day, day and night, to mean the entire cycle of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [unlike any ordinary period of time]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 14:7 (#4)
content:
לֹא־י֣וֹם וְ⁠לֹא־לָ֑יְלָה וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה לְ⁠עֵֽת־עֶ֖רֶב יִֽהְיֶה־אֽוֹר

"not day and not night. And it will happen, at the time of evening there will be light"

Zechariah states And it will happen here to indicate a contrast between the darkness that would normally be expected at evening and the light that will be present instead. In your translation, do not try to explain or fix this contract, instead indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [there will be neither day nor night, but at the time of evening there will be light]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Zechariah 14:8 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠קַּ֥יִץ וּ⁠בָ⁠חֹ֖רֶף

"in the summer and in the winter"

Zechariah is using the two main seasons of the year, the summer and the winter, to mean the whole year. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all year long]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 14:8 (#2)
content:
מַֽיִם־חַיִּים֙

"living waters"

Zechariah is using living waters as a common expression of the culture to mean “fresh water that flows continually” and “water that gives life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continually flowing fresh streams] or [life-giving water]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:9 (#1)
content:
יִהְיֶ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה אֶחָ֖ד וּ⁠שְׁמ֥⁠וֹ אֶחָֽד

"Yahweh will be one, and his name, one"

The implication is that people everywhere will worship Yahweh alone and honor him alone as God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will be the only God whom people worship, and his name, the only name that they honor]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 14:9 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠שְׁמ֥⁠וֹ אֶחָֽד

"and his name, one"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that his name will be one, that is, unique. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his name will be one, meaning unique]

See: Ellipsis

title: Zechariah 14:9 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠שְׁמ֥⁠וֹ

"and his name"

Here, his name represents Yahweh himself and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his reputation will be unique]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 14:10 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠גֶּ֣בַע לְ⁠רִמּ֔וֹן נֶ֖גֶב יְרֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם

"from Geba to Rimmon, south of Jerusalem"

Zechariah is using the two extremes of the land of Judah, Geba in the north and Rimmon in the south, to mean all of the land between them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from one end of the land to the other]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 14:10 (#2)
content:
יִסּ֨וֹב כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֤רֶץ כָּ⁠עֲרָבָה֙

"All the land will turn like the Arabah"

The point of this comparison is that just as the Arabah is a flat plain, so the land around Jerusalem will become flat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [All the land will become as flat as the Arabah plain]

See: Simile

title: Zechariah 14:10 (#3)
content:
וְֽ⁠רָאֲמָה֩ וְ⁠יָשְׁבָ֨ה תַחְתֶּ֜י⁠הָ

"But it will rise up and will dwell in its place"

The pronoun it refers to Jerusalem, not to the land that will become flat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But Jerusalem will rise up and will dwell in its place]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 14:10 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠מִ⁠שַּׁ֣עַר בִּנְיָמִ֗ן עַד־מְק֞וֹם שַׁ֤עַר הָֽ⁠רִאשׁוֹן֙ עַד־שַׁ֣עַר הַ⁠פִּנִּ֔ים וּ⁠מִגְדַּ֣ל חֲנַנְאֵ֔ל עַ֖ד יִקְבֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ

"from the Gate of Benjamin to the place of the First Gate, to the Gate of the Corners, and {from} the Tower of Hananel to the winepresses of the king"

The words the Gate of Benjamin, the First Gate, the Gate of the Corners, and the Tower of Hananel are the names of places in Jerusalem.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Zechariah 14:10 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠מִ⁠שַּׁ֣עַר בִּנְיָמִ֗ן עַד־מְק֞וֹם שַׁ֤עַר הָֽ⁠רִאשׁוֹן֙ עַד־שַׁ֣עַר הַ⁠פִּנִּ֔ים וּ⁠מִגְדַּ֣ל חֲנַנְאֵ֔ל עַ֖ד יִקְבֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ

"from the Gate of Benjamin to the place of the First Gate, to the Gate of the Corners, and {from} the Tower of Hananel to the winepresses of the king"

Zechariah is referring to all of Jerusalem by naming two extremes, the Gate of Benjamin and the winepresses of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the whole city]

See: Merism

title: Zechariah 14:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יָ֣שְׁבוּ בָ֔⁠הּ

"And they will dwell in it"

The pronoun they refers to the people of Jerusalem, and the pronoun it refers to the city of Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And her people will dwell in Jerusalem]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 14:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠חֵ֖רֶם לֹ֣א יִֽהְיֶה־ע֑וֹד

"and there will not again be destruction"

The implication is that enemies will never again devote Jerusalem to complete destruction in war. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and no enemy will ever again devote it to destruction]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 14:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠חֵ֖רֶם לֹ֣א יִֽהְיֶה־ע֑וֹד

"and there will not again be destruction"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of destruction, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and no one will destroy it again]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 14:11 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יָשְׁבָ֥ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם לָ⁠בֶֽטַח

"and Jerusalem will dwell in security"

Jerusalem is spoken of as a living thing. By referring to the city in this way, the meaning is that its name represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Jerusalem will dwell in security]

See: Metonymy

title: Zechariah 14:11 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠יָשְׁבָ֥ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם לָ⁠בֶֽטַח

"and Jerusalem will dwell in security"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of security, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and Jerusalem will dwell securely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 14:12 (#1)
content:
בְּשָׂר֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠הוּא֙ עֹמֵ֣ד עַל־רַגְלָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠עֵינָי⁠ו֙ תִּמַּ֣קְנָה בְ⁠חֹֽרֵי⁠הֶ֔ן וּ⁠לְשׁוֹנ֖⁠וֹ תִּמַּ֥ק בְּ⁠פִי⁠הֶֽם

"his flesh & while he is standing on his feet, and his eyes will rot in their sockets, and his tongue will rot in their mouth"

The pronouns he and his refer to each individual among the peoples who waged war against Jerusalem, while the pronoun their refers to those same peoples together as a group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [each person’s flesh will rot away while he is standing on his feet, and his eyes will rot in their sockets, and his tongue will rot in his mouth]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Zechariah 14:12 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הוּא֙ עֹמֵ֣ד עַל־רַגְלָ֔י⁠ו

"while he is standing on his feet"

Zechariah is using while he is standing on his feet as a common expression of the culture to mean “while he is still alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while he is yet living]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:13 (#1)
content:
מְהֽוּמַת־יְהוָ֛ה רַבָּ֖ה

"a great tumult of Yahweh"

Zechariah is using the possessive form a great tumult of Yahweh to describe a tumult that Yahweh himself will cause. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a great tumult that Yahweh sends]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 14:13 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הֶחֱזִ֗יקוּ אִ֚ישׁ יַ֣ד רֵעֵ֔⁠הוּ

"and each man will seize the hand of his neighbor"

Here the masculine term man could refer to: (1) soldiers of the enemy armies, Alternate translation: [and each soldier will seize the hand of his neighbor] or (2) have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and each person will seize the hand of his neighbor]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Zechariah 14:13 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֶחֱזִ֗יקוּ אִ֚ישׁ יַ֣ד רֵעֵ֔⁠הוּ

"and each man will seize the hand of his neighbor"

Zechariah is using each man will seize the hand of his neighbor as a common expression of the culture to mean that people will panic and attack one another in confusion. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everyone will grab hold of the person next to them in panic] or [everyone will turn against the person next to them in confusion]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:13 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עָלְתָ֥ה יָד֖⁠וֹ עַל־יַ֥ד רֵעֵֽ⁠הוּ

"and his hand will go up against the hand of his neighbor"

Zechariah is using his hand will go up against as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will attack.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will attack his neighbor]

See: Idiom

title: Zechariah 14:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠גַ֨ם־יְהוּדָ֔ה תִּלָּחֵ֖ם בִּ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם

"And also Judah will fight at Jerusalem"

The implication is that the people of Judah will take part in this battle. This could mean: (1) that they will fight at Jerusalem alongside its people against the nations. Alternate translation: [And also Judah will join Jerusalem in fighting against the nations] or (2) that they will fight against Jerusalem along with the nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Judah will also join the nations in fighting against Jerusalem]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Zechariah 14:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אֻסַּף֩ חֵ֨יל כָּל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֜ם סָבִ֗יב

"And the wealth of all the nations around will be gathered"

The expression will be gathered is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they will collect the wealth of all the nations around]

See: Active or Passive

title: Zechariah 14:14 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠רֹ֥ב מְאֹֽד

"in very great abundance"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of abundance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in extremely large amounts]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Zechariah 14:15 (#1)
content:
מַגֵּפַ֣ת הַ⁠סּ֗וּס הַ⁠פֶּ֨רֶד֙ הַ⁠גָּמָ֣ל וְ⁠הַ⁠חֲמ֔וֹר

"the plague of the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey"

Zechariah is using the possessive form the plague of the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey to describe the plague that will strike those animals. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the plague that will strike the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey]

See: Possession

title: Zechariah 14:15 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠סּ֗וּס הַ⁠פֶּ֨רֶד֙ הַ⁠גָּמָ֣ל וְ⁠הַ⁠חֲמ֔וֹר

"the horse, the mule, the camel, and the donkey"

Zechariah is not referring to a specific horse, mule, camel, or donkey. He means horses, mules, camels, and donkeys in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the horses, mules, camels, and donkeys]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Zechariah 14:16 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠הִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֺת֙ לְ⁠מֶ֨לֶךְ֙

"to bow down to the King"

Bowing down before someone was a symbolic action by which a person showed honor and submission to a ruler. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [to bow down in honor and submission to the King]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Zechariah 14:16 (#2)
content:
אֶת־חַ֥ג הַ⁠סֻּכּֽוֹת

"the Festival of Booths"

The Festival of Booths is a kind of yearly celebration during which the Israelites lived in temporary shelters for a week to remember how their ancestors lived after they came out of Egypt. If your readers would not be familiar with what the Festival of Booths is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the yearly festival of living in temporary huts]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Zechariah 14:17 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא־יַעֲלֶ֜ה מֵ⁠אֵ֨ת מִשְׁפְּח֤וֹת הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ֙ אֶל־יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לְ⁠הִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֔ת לְ⁠מֶ֖לֶךְ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת וְ⁠לֹ֥א עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם יִהְיֶ֥ה הַ⁠גָּֽשֶׁם
